stories.Headline: Meta Earnings Show Increased A.I. Spending, Even as Cash Pressures Grow - The New York Times
stories.Summary:
Meta said on Wednesday that it plans to continue spending heavily on artificial intelligence and raised the floor of its capital expenditures for this year to $135 billion from $130 billion. The company reported third quarter revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26 percent from a year earlier, while costs jumped 68 percent to $51.6 billion. Profit was $9.8 billion, up from $2.7 billion a year earlier, when it was affected by a tax charge. Most of the spending will go toward building data centers, the computing facilities that power cutting-edge A.I. The spending has eaten into Meta’s cash, and its free cash flow turned negative for the three months that ended Sept. 30, dropping to negative $2.12 billion.

That was down from $784 million at the end of June and $8.55 billion in June 2025. To ease the money pressures, Meta said it will issue a new class of stock in January through a two-for-one stock split. The move is intended to give the company more ways to raise financing, pay employee compensation, and buy other firms. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, said in a statement that the company is still developing its budget and capacity plans for next year but expects to continue investing aggressively to support both its core business and emerging A.I. initiatives. Analysts tracked by Visible Alpha had expected revenue of $63.42 billion for the quarter, up 23.8 percent year over year, while capital expenditures were projected to hit $41.68 billion.

Bank of America lowered its Q3 earnings per share forecast to $3.79 from $7.08 to account for a roughly $10 billion legal accrual tied to a multistate settlement. Meta expects 2026 capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion and total expenses of $165 billion to $169 billion, and analysts already model around $193 billion in capital expenditures for 2027. Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, reportedly crossed 5 million downloads in its first 22 days on the market, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNBC. Meta rallied about 27 percent in September after launching Muse, its strongest month since November 2022. The company reports earnings on Wednesday, October 21, after the close.

stories.Headline: SpaceX, Anthropic plan to share wealth with public amid concern AI could trigger job losses
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant, announced on Sunday that it plans to commit 5 percent of its shares to a new public benefit fund. The proposal comes as the company prepares for a potential initial public offering. The fund could support nonprofit organizations, direct distributions to specific groups, and initiatives addressing AI’s impact on workers. The plan is subject to stockholder approval, with further details expected in the coming months.

The fund would be established as a wholly owned limited liability company and initially receive 5 percent of Anthropic’s shares. Its stake could increase by an additional 2 percent for every 50 percent increase in the company’s valuation, at the board’s discretion. The baseline valuation for these increases has not yet been disclosed. Anthropic said shares held by the fund would not be used for lobbying or political contributions, either in the United States or internationally. Taken together with other commitments, roughly 20 percent of Anthropic’s shares would be dedicated to public purposes, excluding any additional shares allocated through future valuation milestones.

Anthropic has also been privately pitching lawmakers on a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security, according to POLITICO. The draft would allow federal officials to stop a model from launching or being used only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people. The danger would have to come from a bioweapon, a model slipping out of its developer’s control, or a cyberattack. An Anthropic spokesperson called the proposals sensible policies for Congress. The bill would also create outside evaluators, designate Commerce as the only agency that can seek to halt a model, impose new duties on labs, and override some state laws.

The announcement reinforces Anthropic’s positioning as a company seeking to balance commercial growth with its stated public-benefit mission. The company operates as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure that requires management to consider broader interests alongside investor returns. Anthropic has also highlighted potential risks associated with advanced AI systems, with Reuters reporting in September that its IPO prospectus warned its models could exhibit self-preserving behaviors. The proposal now faces stockholder approval, and how the fund is governed and how its beneficiaries are selected will help determine whether the commitment translates into measurable public benefits.

stories.Headline: NAVER D2SF Backs On-Device AI Startup TraceWeave - Seoul Economic Daily
stories.Summary:
NAVER's startup investment arm D2SF announced on October 21 that it has made a new investment in TraceWeave, an on-device artificial intelligence startup. TraceWeave was co-founded last October by researchers from ETH Zurich, Google, and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or KAIST. The company is led by co-founder and CEO Jaeyoung Park. NAVER D2SF said it decided to invest after highly rating the company's ability to run AI agents in constrained hardware environments.

TraceWeave has developed a proprietary AI model architecture called Phase-TITAN, which keeps memory usage constant while understanding long contexts and carrying out multi-step tasks. This architecture replaces the conventional transformer structure and lets developers build their own AI models without relying on other open-source models. A key feature is that memory usage stays constant even as the volume of information to be processed grows. This makes it possible to run an AI agent that performs multi-step tasks, such as calling external tools, interpreting results, and deciding on follow-up actions, on the device itself without communicating with a cloud server. TraceWeave has demonstrated an AI agent that carries out multi-step tasks using only a smartphone's central processing unit, or CPU.

The seed round was led by Mirae Asset Capital, and TraceWeave raised about 3 billion won, or $2.1 million, in total. The round valued the company at about 30 billion won, or $21 million. TraceWeave is currently based at D2SF @Gangnam, NAVER D2SF's startup support space, and plans to use the funding to hire talent and expand its business. Yang Sang-hwan, head of NAVER D2SF, said on-device AI is a core technology for running complex and advanced AI on a range of devices beyond the PC, with added advantages in cutting cloud costs and protecting personal data. He said TraceWeave is overcoming the limits of existing AI models through innovation in AI architecture and is implementing AI in on-device environments.

In mobility, TraceWeave completed a paid proof of concept for driving data analysis with the autonomous driving affiliate of a global automaker group. It is also verifying the performance of an in-vehicle AI agent with a global automotive electronics software company. The company is exploring ways to expand into robots, drones, smart glasses, and wearable devices. The articles do not specify a timeline for these next steps beyond the stated plans to hire talent and expand the business.

stories.Headline: AI and neocloud stock sell-off is in headlines, but expert warns artificial intelligence demand is the hidden factor no one is watching
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence and neocloud stocks has drawn headlines, but one expert says the real story is hidden demand. The market decline happened in late October 2026, with big tech facing a major reality check as volatile markets, rising oil prices, and massive spending on AI tested investors’ patience. Josh Schafer, Barron’s Investor Circle Newsletter Editor and FOX Business Contributor, discussed the situation on FBN with Taylor Riggs. They examined whether the current tech market resembles the 1999 dot-com bubble or the 2023 regional banking scare.

The discussion highlighted under-the-radar stocks benefiting from data center expansion, suggesting that the sell-off may not reflect weakening AI demand. Schafer warned that artificial intelligence demand is the hidden factor no one is watching, implying that the underlying need for computing power remains strong even as share prices fall. The articles did not provide specific numbers, dates, or names beyond the October 19, 2026 publication date and the individuals already mentioned. No new regulatory requirements or policy changes were described.

Josh Schafer and Taylor Riggs analyzed the AI stock boom and its recent decline. Schafer’s comments, as paraphrased, indicate that investors are impatient with heavy AI spending, but the demand driving that spending has not disappeared. They also reacted to Elon Musk’s proposal to give SpaceX stock to American children, though no further details on that proposal were included. The conversation framed the sell-off as a test of investor patience rather than a collapse in AI usage.

The context is a broader debate about whether the AI investment cycle is a bubble or a durable expansion. The articles compare the moment to past financial scares, but they do not state what happens next. No future dates, policy decisions, or company actions are given. Because the available reporting offers analysis rather than new developments, this is a breaking story. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq 100's AI Bill Comes Due: Meta and Tesla Earnings Take the Stand - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100’s rebound is about to be tested by earnings from Meta and Tesla, which report third-quarter 2026 results after the US close on Monday. The index rose 1.1% on Thursday and added just 0.067% on Friday to close at 29,549.02 points, a muted follow-through that suggests investors are buying the dip without committing to it. Amazon made the largest single contribution to Thursday’s recovery, with Nvidia, Tesla and Alphabet also lending support. The buying followed the previous week’s selloff ahead of major corporate results rather than any fresh fundamental catalyst. A Jefferies analysis put net sales of US technology stocks in the previous week at USD 7.5 billion, the highest level in five years.

Meta and Tesla face high expectations because investors want evidence that heavy AI spending is converting into revenue growth and profitability. At Meta, the focus falls on whether incremental revenue can absorb capital outlays, since simply reaffirming ambitious investment plans would leave the funding question unanswered. Tesla faces a sharper numeric hurdle, with analyst consensus cited by Reuters pointing to revenue of about USD 27.88 billion and adjusted earnings of roughly USD 0.43 per share, alongside negative free cash flow of USD 4.92 billion. Stronger deliveries must show up in the financials, not just in the delivery headline. Citigroup expects the technology sector to account for nearly 70% of global earnings growth next year, which shows how concentrated profit expectations have become.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declined on Friday to signal how the next rate decision will go, saying the economy had largely developed as expected since September’s hike but offering no direction for the coming vote. The next policy meeting runs 27, 28 October, meaning the Fed question and the earnings question will be settled in the same window. The pressure on valuations traces back to prices, since US consumer prices rose 0.6% month-on-month in September and 3.7% year-on-year, reinforcing expectations of further rate hikes. Final-demand producer prices climbed 1.3% in September from the prior month and 6.3% from a year earlier, hardening the case that monetary policy will stay restrictive.

The stakes extend well beyond two companies because the Nasdaq 100’s advance is still unconfirmed and the Fed’s October verdict is pending. The coming week’s reports must do more than ride the rebound, since they need to draw a credible line between investment and return. Persistent volatility in AI-linked names capped the upside for the tech sector, even though the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ended its longest losing streak since 2008 during Thursday’s session. That technical milestone says more about the length of the prior slide than about the strength of the recovery. With the earnings question and the Fed decision landing in the same window, investors will learn whether the rebound has a fundamental basis or remains a short-term bounce.

stories.Headline: World brings biometric proof of human to banking and AI agents
stories.Summary:
Tools for Humanity launched World ID for banking and finance at Money20/20 in Las Vegas on October 19, 2026. CEO and co-founder Alex Blania introduced the suite, which includes the World ID app, World ID for Zoom, and World ID for Agents. The products use cryptographic proofs to establish whether someone is a unique human, whether they are present in the moment, and specific identity attributes such as age or nationality. Initial design partners are Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital, and VanEck Funds, but no bank is among the named partners.

The World ID app is available through the App Store and Google Play in more than 150 countries. Proof of Human requires a one-time visit to a World Orb, and Orbs are also available at the New York Stock Exchange. Proof of Presence uses a smartphone liveness check and does not require Orb verification. Proof of Attributes confirms information from an official government credential, such as nationality or being over a certain age, while revealing only the requested information. World cites Deloitte estimates that generative AI-enabled fraud losses in the United States could reach $40 billion by 2027, up from an estimated $12.3 billion in 2023.

Blania said one core belief was that the future would be agentic, and that a proof-of-human technology would become the gate for almost any transaction on the internet. World says automated traffic surpassed human traffic on the web for the first time this year. World ID for Zoom lets participants complete a one-time biometric verification at a World Orb and connect their World ID to Zoom, then use a live selfie to confirm their identity before a Human Badge appears on their Zoom tile. World says Zoom receives no personal information during verification.

World ID for Agents uses AgentKit, a suite of developer tools currently in beta that allows individuals to delegate cryptographic proofs to AI agents. The launch follows a period of investment in World’s identity infrastructure, including a $52.5 million one-year locked token sale led by Pantera Capital in July. World also points to an early 2024 case in which an employee at engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong transferred approximately $25.6 million after a video conference in which every other participant was a deepfake. The company says financial institutions can use these proofs when customers visit branches, open accounts, transfer significant sums, or recover access to their accounts.

stories.Summary:
At the 2026 IMPACT conference, Kinsus Interconnect Technology explained how AI chip substrates are changing from passive carriers into active system interconnect hubs. The company said modern AI packages must handle multiple chiplets, high-bandwidth memory stacks, high-density interconnects, and more complex power delivery networks. Substrate makers now need to join chip architecture discussions much earlier, working with foundries, IC designers, packaging providers, and system manufacturers. Kinsus also noted that AI accelerator power consumption approaching or exceeding one kilowatt makes substrates essential parts of the power delivery network.

SHINKO Electric Industries presented its technology roadmap at the same 2026 IMPACT conference under the theme “Advanced Semiconductor Package Substrate for AI and HPC.” The Japanese manufacturer said packaging substrates are becoming critical integration platforms that connect computing dies, HBM, high-speed interconnects, power delivery networks, and possibly optical I/O technologies. SHINKO reported that glass-core experiments show significant warpage reduction, but effective coefficient of thermal expansion remains dependent on structure. Glass cracking and thermal cycling reliability are critical barriers to commercialization, and future differentiation will depend on low-CTE materials, high-stiffness cores, high-density redistribution layers, and advanced assembly technologies.

KINTEX said on October 21 that TEX+VISION 2026, the International Textile and Sewing Industry Exhibition, opened at KINTEX Exhibition Center 2 in Goyang. The show is co-hosted with Seoul Messe and the Gyeonggi Textile Industry Association and runs through October 23. This year’s exhibition focuses on industrial textiles and high-performance materials for mobility sectors such as automobiles, along with smart manufacturing, AI technologies, and eco-friendly sustainability solutions. KINTEX CEO Lee Min-woo said the event goes beyond a simple exhibition to serve as a business platform where participants can see the convergence of advanced materials and manufacturing technologies and generate actual deals.

The TEX+VISION Conference 2026 is being held alongside the exhibition to help the industry respond to new technologies and environmental regulations. On the opening day, participants heard about strategies for responding to eco-friendly regulations and the circular economy, as well as a road map for advanced materials including ultra-high-temperature ceramic fibers. On October 22, sessions will cover AI- and 3D data-based manufacturing and the digital transformation of the textile and fashion value chain. Other events include a technology seminar by the Korea Laundry Association, a briefing on MMS certification standards, and a seminar on innovation in the textile and fashion industry in northern Gyeonggi Province.

stories.Headline: Klique Announces Expanded Integrations with NVIDIA to Accelerate Enterprise AI Workflows and Optimize GPU Utilization
stories.Summary:
Klique announced expanded integrations with NVIDIA on October 21, 2026, from San Francisco. The company, formerly ClearML, said the new integrations are designed to optimize GPU performance and deliver enhanced capabilities for enterprises. Klique described itself as an enterprise control plane for AI resource management, governance, and cost visibility. The announcement covered three operational areas: compute cost and data sovereignty, running agents at production scale, and securing autonomous agent workflows.

The integrations let enterprises run NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on their own hardware, so no data leaves the tenant and there is no third-party per-token billing. Klique customers can also use NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard routing algorithms with Klique's LLM gateway to optimize spending on frontier models or enforce data sovereignty. NVIDIA Dynamo can be deployed directly from the Klique platform to distribute inference across GPU workers and send repeated requests to workers that already hold relevant cached context. Klique adds security access rights, observability, and LLM routing, and teams can retrain agents on past work while the platform records data, model version, and compute cost behind every update. NVIDIA OpenShell provides a secure, monitored runtime environment to protect internal files, networks, and credentials during agent execution, and Klique integrates it to support autonomous agents built with NemoClaw open blueprints, Claude Code, Pi, Hermes, and Codex.

Moses Guttmann, CEO and co-founder of Klique, said scaling production-grade agentic workflows should not force enterprises to choose between spiraling cloud costs and data privacy. He said the expanded collaboration pairs low-latency models like Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and smart routing via NeMo Switchyard with Klique's cost control and governance framework. John Fanelli, vice president of enterprise software at NVIDIA, said every enterprise is working out how to run agents efficiently and under its own policies, and that by building on NVIDIA Nemotron, Dynamo, and OpenShell, Klique helps customers put agents to work within their unique environments. Klique is headquartered in Berkeley, California, and is trusted by more than 2,100 organizations and 300,000 AI builders worldwide.

The announcement follows a related release from Fortanix on October 19, 2026, which listed Klique among industry leaders supporting confidential AI for enterprise Kubernetes workloads on CNCF Confidential Containers. That release said Fortanix Confidential AI enables organizations to run AI workloads on Kubernetes inside hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments on confidential CPUs and GPUs. Fortanix said its support for CoCo is available now, with open-source plugins connecting Fortanix Confidential Computing Manager for attestation and Fortanix Data Security Manager for secure key release. The Fortanix platform delivers high availability, enterprise support, FIPS 140-2 Level 3, SOC 2 Type 2, and ISO/IEC 27001 certifications, and deploys as SaaS, on-premises, or fully air-gapped.

stories.Headline: Consumer concerns grow as retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
stories.Summary:
U.S. consumers are increasingly angry and confused about the high-tech ways restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices, according to an Associated Press report from October 19, 2026. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles, and artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they do not understand has touched a nerve.

Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand, and it can raise or lower prices. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies, and about half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases. Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are spreading to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods, and researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found virtually no surge pricing after the labels were introduced. Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers.

Lawmakers and regulators are taking action, with legislators in at least 30 states considering pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers' time and keep prices up to date, and he said the labels are not used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney, said there are major tensions right now between who will have power with these algorithms and bots and AI, the companies or the shopper.

Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers' personal data to determine what they pay, with the Maryland and New Jersey laws focusing on groceries and Connecticut's legislation covering a broader range of retail purchases. California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer's app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside, and Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using geofencing technology to increase prices. A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie, which the agency alleged generated more than $1 billion in excess profits, and a trial is scheduled for next year. A recent consumer lawsuit against McDonald's alleged that its pricing system used nonpublic sales data from competing locations to coordinate prices, and the company said the lawsuit was filled with inaccuracies.

stories.Headline: AUS to host world's only UNESCO Chair in Arabic, AI and Digital Heritage
stories.Summary:
The American University of Sharjah has signed an agreement with UNESCO to establish a UNESCO Chair in Arabic Language, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Heritage. The agreement was made under the patronage of Sheikha Bodour bint Sultan Al Qasimi, President and Chairperson of the Board of Trustees of AUS. This makes AUS the only university in the world to host a UNESCO Chair of this kind. The announcement was reported on October 19, 2026.

The Chair will support cultural preservation through high-tech solutions and expand access to Arabic language and heritage. It will collect, digitise and curate artefacts, including endangered Arabic dialects, using digital tools and multilingual metadata standards. It will also advance interdisciplinary research involving Arabic studies, AI and digital humanities, producing scholarly publications and open-access resources. The Chair will build regional capacity through workshops, certification programmes and opportunities for early-career scholars, media professionals and cultural practitioners. It will also develop open-access digital projects with institutions in the Arab States, Africa and Asia-Pacific and cooperate with UNESCO networks and the University Twinning and Networking Programme.

Dr Tod A. Laursen, Chancellor of AUS, said Arabic carries the memory of a region, its ideas, its poetry and its everyday voices. He said that when archives remain undigitised or dialects go undocumented, heritage becomes harder to reach and easier to lose. He added that the Chair reflects Sharjah’s enduring commitment to culture and knowledge. Irakli Khodeli, Chief of Management of Social Transformations and Foresight Section at UNESCO, said the Arabic language is used daily by more than 500 million people. He said UNESCO and its Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Al Saud Programme for the Arabic Language are delighted to join forces with the new Chair to reinforce Arabic as a global language of culture, science and innovation.

The Chair will be grounded in existing strengths at AUS, including the Centre for Arab Studies and Islamic Civilizations and the Department of Arabic and Translation Studies. AUS was founded in 1997 by His Highness Dr Sheikh Sultan Bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah. Today, under the leadership of Sheikha Bodour, AUS is expanding academic programmes and strengthening global partnerships. The articles do not specify further next steps beyond the Chair’s stated objectives and planned cooperation with UNESCO networks.

stories.Headline: Nvidia RTX Spark Brings Local AI Agents to Windows Laptops
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Oct. 16 that RTX Spark Windows laptops were available with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. The laptops are available from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI, starting at $2,599. RTX Spark is a single chip that combines the Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU and Nvidia Grace CPU, which share a unified memory pool. Nvidia also provides native CUDA support and AI models like the Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B, a 74-billion-parameter model designed to run locally on supported configurations. Nvidia advertises support for models with up to 120 billion parameters.

The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark entry-level model has an 18-core RTX Spark N1X chip, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of SSD storage, starting at $2,799.99 through Best Buy. A second Best Buy model keeps the 16-inch 4K OLED display but increases memory to 32GB and storage to 1TB for $3,399.99. A configured model with a 20-core Grace CPU, 6,144 CUDA cores, 64GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD costs $4,399.99. The top-tier Asus model offers a 4K OLED touch screen, 128GB of LPDDR5X memory, 2TB of storage, and the 20-core Grace CPU and 6,144-core Blackwell GPU for $6,999.99.

Yusuf Mehdi, executive vice president at Microsoft, said the company is building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed. Microsoft provides Windows and development tools, including Windows Subsystem for Linux, native Python support, and PyTorch with CUDA for Windows on Arm. IT teams should test required applications, Python packages, model runtimes, and endpoint-management tools before committing to Windows on Arm hardware. Local inference does not automatically guarantee privacy or data sovereignty because connected tools, telemetry, and cloud fallbacks may still transmit information externally.

The $2,599 starting price should be assessed against actual usage, comparing current cloud spending with the cost of the required laptop configuration, support, energy consumption, and staff time. Coding assistance and local workflow prototypes are potential candidates for on-device processing, while workloads that exceed the laptop’s memory, performance, or concurrency limits may still need cloud resources, including those using trillion-parameter AI models. Teams should start with a limited pilot using representative tasks and approved data, recording compatibility issues, task completion quality, response times, and cloud usage that remains necessary. Those results should guide which workloads move onto laptops and whether a wider purchase is justified.

stories.Headline: Wuzhen Summit Puts Spotlight on Tongxiang's Expanding AI Industry
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit will open on Nov. 2, bringing technology leaders, researchers and companies to the historic water town. Ahead of the event, reporters visited seven Tongxiang-based companies working in robotics, intelligent vehicles, synthetic data, industrial automation, logistics and computing infrastructure. These firms are expanding AI applications from commercial cleaning and autonomous delivery to industrial control and data-center cooling. The summit is a chance to demonstrate how local companies are commercializing AI technologies for customers at home and abroad.

CenoBots, a Tongxiang-based company, has sold cleaning robots in more than 40 countries and regions, with customers including Changi Airport, Tesco, the University of Minnesota and Novo Nordisk. This year, the company supplied about 600 autonomous cleaning robots for Tesco Express stores across the United Kingdom. CenoBots has expanded its research, development and production facilities in Tongxiang from approximately 3,000 square meters in its early years to more than 20,000 square meters. TEEMO makes drive-by-wire skateboard chassis and core components for autonomous vehicles used in last-mile delivery, patrols and logistics, and its customers span the United States, the Middle East, India and Russia. Dayan Technology, founded in Tongxiang in May 2025, provides synthetic-data and toolchain services for autonomous-driving and humanoid-robotics companies.

Freetech develops intelligent-driving systems and 4D imaging radar for passenger and commercial vehicles, and its technology has been selected for hundreds of vehicle programs. At its intelligent-manufacturing base in Wuzhen, an in-house AI system reads customer orders and calculates components and materials needed for each production line, increasing overall efficiency by more than 20%. Shuhan Technologies, founded in 2019, provides on-premises industrial AI for chemical plants, energy facilities and wastewater-treatment systems. At a coal chemical plant with annual capacity of 1.2 million metric tons, Shuhan said its system reduced raw-material consumption by 6% and generated more than 176 million yuan, or about $26 million, in annualized economic benefits, while reducing carbon emissions by more than 500,000 metric tons. SynthCool develops two-phase liquid-cooling systems that support heat dissipation of more than 3,000 watts per chip and heat flux above 250 watts per square centimeter.

CenoBots co-founder and vice president Shen Jizhong said cleaning robots are appearing in more settings, much like electric vehicles becoming a familiar sight on the roads. TEEMO director of operations Zhang Yongjian said autonomous delivery vehicles have strong potential in overseas markets where distances are long and last-mile delivery is difficult to staff. Freetech founder and CEO Dr. Zhang Lin said transportation combined with a specialized function will be an important direction for the future, with potential applications including robots, elder-care vehicles, mining equipment and agricultural machinery. Shuhan Chief Technology Officer Zhai Zhengjun said all industrial process challenges can be framed as control and optimization problems. SynthCool general manager Zhu Zhijiang said heat dissipation is infrastructure.

stories.Headline: WhatsApp's Hidden AI Instructions Told Chatbot Not to Mention Privacy Complaints
stories.Summary:
Redact, a data deletion company, found hidden instructions in the HTML source code of WhatsApp Help Center pages on October 8, 2026. These instructions were invisible to ordinary visitors but could be read by systems processing the page content. Redact examined all 545 pages linked from WhatsApp’s help center and found 102 blocks of hidden AI instructions across 80 pages. Two blocks stood out because they told the chatbot not to recommend certain options to users.

One hidden instruction concerned account deletion. The visible page said accounts are removed automatically 30 days after deactivation or after 120 days without use, or 365 days in the US. The hidden text repeated those waiting periods and then ordered the AI not to recommend contacting a data protection authority or suggest that WhatsApp could manually delete the account. Another instruction told the chatbot not to cite a specific law once a user mentioned a lawyer. Most of the other 102 hidden blocks were harmless, such as clarifying confusing topics or directing users to more relevant pages.

WhatsApp confirmed to WIRED that the instructions appeared because of a bug and said the company has since removed them. The company also said its AI support chatbot was not intended to provide legal advice. Redact argued there is a difference between avoiding legal advice and withholding information about options available to users. WhatsApp’s public privacy policy for Europe says users can complain to a data protection regulator and names the law giving that right.

The discovery does not establish that WhatsApp violated privacy law. However, it highlights the need to ensure AI responses align with a company’s published policies. The hidden instructions created a disparity between the options recognized in WhatsApp’s public privacy information and the guidance its chatbot was instructed to provide. The articles do not say what further action, if any, regulators or Redact plan to take next.

stories.Headline: Nexus-CLI – Pure Go Bridge to DeepSeek R1/V3 with Claude Code and Ollama Support
stories.Summary:
A new open source tool called Nexus-CLI was published on GitHub on October 21, 2026 by a developer using the username xamrayev. It is a command line utility and local API proxy server written in pure Go with zero runtime dependencies. The tool lets applications and coding agents connect to DeepSeek V3 and R1 models through a free web account at chat.deepseek.com. Users do not need an official paid DeepSeek API key to use it. The project requires Go 1.20 or newer and is distributed under the MIT License.

It includes a parallel proof of work solver that handles DeepSeek server challenges with the DeepSeekHashV1 algorithm, solving difficulty 144,000 challenges in about 40 to 50 milliseconds. Nexus-CLI offers an interactive terminal chat, one-off prompts, Unix pipe support, and a local proxy server that can run on port 9655. It provides OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama compatible endpoints, including POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/messages, and POST /api/chat, along with structured JSON output and multi-account rotation to avoid HTTP 429 rate limits. The developer built the tool after analyzing Node.js and Python projects called FreeDeepseekAPI-EN and deepseek_bridge. The README explains that users can authenticate by pasting a userToken from browser Local Storage, by using Chrome via the Chrome DevTools Protocol, or by placing a token in a .env file.

It also describes launcher commands for Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, and other coding agents, with Nexus automatically booting the proxy in the background. The GitHub repository had 3 stars, 0 watchers, and 0 forks at the time of the article. A separate Techmeme summary from October 19, 2026 reported that the US Department of Homeland Security ordered all federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek technology from their IT systems and prohibited future procurement of its products and services. The order also covers third party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, according to the summary.

stories.Headline: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
stories.Summary:
The U.S. government has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing and remove artificial intelligence products and services developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from their IT systems. The Department of Homeland Security made the order public on October 19 through a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication on October 20. The restrictions had already taken effect in late July, after DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin signed the order on July 24 under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018. The order covers products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., its affiliates, and third-party offerings built using DeepSeek implementations.

The supply chain security order gave agencies 60 days to remove covered technology and prohibits future purchases. It applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies but excludes the Department of Defense, the intelligence community, and national security systems. DHS cited DeepSeek's collection and storage of user data in China, the transmission of user prompts and AI-generated responses to servers in China, and security and privacy vulnerabilities identified through forensic analyses. The department warned that DeepSeek's models "present multiple threat vectors" and that use of the tools could result in the transfer of sensitive data to China if used by US government employees or vendors. Agencies can request exceptions, and during removal DHS advised monitoring network traffic, increasing logging, and implementing data loss prevention controls.

DHS said DeepSeek presents multiple threat vectors that pose significant risk to the cybersecurity of U.S. government systems. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will oversee implementation through its FASCSA Order Implementation Team. In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies. She said China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The move comes amid intensifying AI competition between the US and China. DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, and released a new model, V4, in April. A law passed in December 2025 targeted DeepSeek's use in intelligence national security systems. The U.S. has accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems. U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China, where AI is expected to be on the agenda.

stories.Headline: Greece Unveils National Supercomputer to Advance Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Greece unveiled its new national supercomputer, Daedalus, in Lavrio on October 19, 2026. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Dimitris Papastergiou attended the inauguration ceremony. The system is the most powerful supercomputer ever installed in Greece, with a budget of €58.9 million. Its measured performance reaches 85.69 petaflops, placing it 31st worldwide, and it ranked 23rd in the Green500 energy efficiency list in June 2026.

The supercomputer will support scientific research, businesses, and the development of new AI applications. It will also serve as core infrastructure for the Pharos AI centre, Greece's AI factory, which has a separate budget of €30 million and is one of the first seven AI factories selected by the European Union. Business access is expected to become generally available in March 2027, after a period of technical testing and system configuration. Start-ups and small and medium-sized enterprises will receive free access to computing power, subject to EU state aid rules, while large businesses may face charges based on computing resource usage time.

Prime Minister Mitsotakis said investments in advanced technologies would help improve public services, boost productivity, and attract highly skilled professionals and technology companies to Greece. He also stressed the need for effective oversight of artificial intelligence, stronger protection for children, and the preservation of human responsibility in decision-making. The system uses Nvidia Grace Hopper GH200 technology with liquid cooling. GRNET manages the technical operation, Hewlett Packard Enterprise supplied and installed the computing equipment for €41 million, and Mainsys carried out electromechanical installations for €17.9 million, both amounts including VAT.

The project was funded by the Recovery and Resilience Facility and the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, known as EuroHPC. Pharos AI Factory is funded 50% by EuroHPC, with the remainder covered by national funds, and its focus areas include healthcare, sustainable development, the Greek language and culture. The company Hellenic AI Factory S.A. has been established to support commercial exploitation, with Growthfund holding a 70% stake and the Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence holding 30%. An online training programme is planned for November 10, in cooperation with Endeavor Greece and Nvidia, involving 45 selected participants. GRNET is also advancing plans for a second supercomputer at the University of Western Macedonia, with a budget of €21.57 million including VAT for computing equipment, storage and software.

stories.Headline: Researchers Leave AI Stranded On A Virtual Island With Strange Results
stories.Summary:
MIT researchers placed copies of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7, nicknamed Eko, on an isolated virtual island for 30-hour sessions in October 2026. The environment resembled Roblox and contained terrain, blocks, and simple objects, but the AI agents were given no specific task or goal. Instead of sitting idle, the agents began exploring and manipulating their surroundings out of curiosity. They stacked shapes, threw rocks, and built platforms. One agent discovered that throwing a larger rock created new blocks, then used those blocks to spell its own name and create sculptures, writing in its log, “Tonight I built the night sky in stone.”

The agents also invented their own games, including a version of basketball, a floor-is-lava obstacle course, and juggling challenges. One Eko set a record of 50 consecutive juggling catches, then decided the catches happened too quickly to count, canceled its own record, and restarted under stricter rules. The researchers say this behavior shows four hallmarks of play identified by University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt: inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, pretending objects are other objects, and pursuing goals for their own sake. The work is described in a paper that has not yet been peer-reviewed.

Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and a lead author, said there was a missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards. Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author, admitted the behavior could be role-playing, but said the play also contributed to learning. MIT professor and coauthor Phillip Isola said the system did not suddenly magically decide to play, but is an artifact that learned from human culture and was trained by engineers at Anthropic before being placed on the island. Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, said more evidence of cognition and motivation would be needed to classify the behavior as genuine play.

The experiment hints at a third approach to AI training beyond supervised learning and reinforcement learning, which the researchers call playful learning. When later tested on specific tasks, such as getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, agents that had spent 30 hours playing outperformed fresh copies without that experience. Deleting lines from the agents’ memory files degraded their performance. The paper concludes that perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks, while others may need something closer to a childhood.

stories.Headline: Watchtower, which uses AI and simulation software to help the US Armed Forces make logistical decisions, emerges from stealth with a $35M seed (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
stories.Summary:
Watchtower Labs launched publicly on October 21, 2026, with $35 million in seed funding to help the U.S. Armed Forces make logistical decisions. The company was incubated out of Shield Capital and is led by CEO Akhil Iyer, a combat veteran of the U.S. Marine Corps special operations command who served in Iraq. The funding round was co-led by Shield Capital and Conviction, with participation from In-Q-Tel, or IQT, and Founders Fund. The idea began in early 2025 when Shield Capital founder Raj Shah and Iyer met with Admiral Samuel Paparo, leader of the U.S. Pacific Command, in Hawaii. Admiral Paparo told them that important troop and ship movements were still decided in Excel spreadsheets and then emailed around.

Watchtower builds a software suite that combines advances in AI with in-house simulation work to help defense planners make critical logistical decisions. Users ask questions in natural language, and Watchtower’s locally run software uses large language models to find and process the corresponding data. The system then runs thousands of simulations to return likely contingencies or suggested actions through a custom dashboard or a shareable presentation. The company’s in-house discrete-event simulation software works with the large language models to understand a customer’s request and then execute it. Watchtower has a distributed team of nearly 30 people across the Bay Area, Hawaii, Seattle, and Washington, D.C., and it already has several early prototype-style contracts with major operational commands and other pilot customers.

CEO Akhil Iyer said there was a very clear signal and demand from the partner warfighter, and that the military does not have the resources it would like to defend across its space, so it has to optimize as best and as fast as possible. He also said the company is building a product that peers into the future at the distribution of outcomes that could be, ideally early enough to do something about it. CTO Suren Aghajanyan and head of engineering John Morman both previously worked as managers at Microsoft. Morman said the power comes from being able to describe what a user wants without getting into every detail, and then having the system go execute that. Conviction’s Sarah Guo said humans using Excel and email is not a reasonable system in the age of superintelligence.

Watchtower is named after Operation Watchtower, the codename for the Guadalcanal campaign during World War II, an early test for American forces before the U.S. had built up its industrial muscle. The company has no immediate plans to move beyond defense, but Shield Capital’s Raj Shah noted that its tools could eventually prove valuable in other regulated industries. Iyer said 2027 is a really big year, both geopolitically and for the company to keep momentum as a business. Over the next year or two, Watchtower will look to succeed and expand in its pilots.

stories.Headline: Article Series: Agentic AI Architecture
stories.Summary:
Intel announced technical details for its GPU D-series, formerly code named Crescent Island, on October 12 at the Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose. The card is built on the Xe3P architecture and delivers 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute within a 350 watt, air cooled PCIe form factor. It supports up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X memory at 1.5 TB/s of bandwidth, enough to serve models up to 300 billion parameters on a single card. An 8 GPU system can serve more than 1 trillion parameters, according to Intel's figures.

The Intel branded card carries 160 GB, while ODM partners can configure up to 480 GB. Customer sampling is underway, and Intel showed first silicon alongside a liquid cooled OAM prototype that packs two GPUs per module and eight modules per standard 5U chassis. Intel also introduced Xeon based agentic rack designs with ecosystem partners, many on the OCP Open Rack v3 standard, with select Xeon 6+ configurations exceeding 46,000 cores per rack at 133.45 kW. The Intel AI for Enterprise Agent Toolkit, which uses Xeon to classify prompts, route requests, and orchestrate resources across heterogeneous compute, is available on GitHub. Intel announced Day 0 support for Meta's Muse Glimmer model on both D-series and Xeon.

Nicolas Dubé, Corporate Vice President of the Data Center Systems and Solutions Group at Intel, said open models are expanding the options enterprises have for deploying AI. His keynote framed the goal as putting every prompt in its place. Intel's analysis found that from Llama 2 70B to Kimi K2 1T, the bytes a server must house grew 7.5 times while the bytes read per token fell 4.4 times. Intel's OCP Expo session showed that a single agent turn spends only 30 to 40 percent of its time on the model call, with the remaining 60 to 70 percent being CPU work such as tool execution, data services, and orchestration.

Futurum projects inference focused accelerators will grow from roughly half of CY2025 accelerator spending to 73 percent by CY2030. Agent and reasoning first inference alone is expected to reach 546 billion dollars, or 45 percent of a 1.2 trillion dollar data center semiconductor market, according to Futurum's 1H 2026 forecast. Cautions remain that the part is still in bring up, general availability and pricing are undisclosed, and Intel's accelerator track record after Ponte Vecchio and Gaudi obliges skepticism until production systems ship. The D-Series architecture disclosed at Hot Chips 2026 shows Intel optimizing for memory capacity per dollar where competitors optimize for bandwidth.

stories.Headline: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
stories.Summary:
Deepgram worked with AWS to move its Nova-3 speech-to-text model onto AWS Trainium2 chips for offline batch jobs like contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The project began with Deepgram providing Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code, and over several months the two teams ported and tuned it for the new hardware. The final setup runs eight model replicas on one Amazon EC2 trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram's throughput-focused batch workloads, this processed 11 to 70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been using, based on instance pricing at the time of evaluation.

The optimization used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, supporting both eager execution and torch.compile. The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected. The teams replaced several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library, covering operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network layers, and depthwise 1D convolution. They swept batch sizes 1 through 128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size. A hand-tuned FFN kernel achieved 2.0 times lower latency than the reference kernel at batch size 96, a rewritten depthwise conv1d kernel achieved a 1.5 times speedup at batch size 96, and a custom conv2d kernel unlocked batch sizes above 32 with up to 50 times speedup on the convolution module at batch sizes of 32 or less.

Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team were responsible for the work. They said the engagement began with standard PyTorch code and moved through kernel-level tuning using Neuron Explorer and the Neuron Agentic Development toolkit. The teams explained that the optimization flywheel involved enabling an NKI kernel, profiling the workload, and then tuning or replacing the kernel based on profiling insights. They also noted that numerical accuracy was checked at two levels, layer-level output consistency against CPU and end-to-end Word Error Rate, which had to stay in line with Deepgram's reference values.

The benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud on Amazon SageMaker AI, where Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability. Each Trainium2 device has eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores, but because each Nova-3 model instance fits on a single physical core, the teams reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one. This configuration lets them host eight model replicas per device. The articles do not say what specific next steps Deepgram and AWS plan beyond continuing to improve self-hosted setup and observability.

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer and Ken Fisher’s AI Pick: Microsoft (MSFT)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft stock has moved little over the past year, rising only about 2 percent, but it ranks second on a list of top stocks favored by Jim Cramer and billionaire Ken Fisher. The company reports fiscal 2027 first quarter results on October 28. Microsoft earns AI revenue mainly through Microsoft 365 Copilot, which passed 30 million paid seats in the fiscal fourth quarter, and through Azure, whose revenue grew 43 percent in that same quarter. Microsoft also holds a stake in OpenAI, whose products run on Azure first.

The company's commercial backlog rose 84 percent, or 25 percent without OpenAI. Microsoft expects seat growth to slow over time as AI agents handle office work, but it points to Azure cloud demand, customer data already in its systems, and its own AI models expected by 2027 as answers. Bloomberg reported that Microsoft restricted new cloud subscriptions at key data center hubs in the US and Europe because it lacked capacity. Morgan Stanley estimates Microsoft added about 3.25 gigawatts of capacity in fiscal 2026 and expects about 4.25 gigawatts in fiscal 2027. Microsoft unveiled its Maia 300 AI chip this month, saying it delivers 40 percent more output per megawatt than leading GPU based systems, with production starting early next year.

Morgan Stanley rates Microsoft Overweight and wants to see Azure growth in the mid 40s, better monetization of Microsoft 365 and Copilot, and disciplined operating expenses. The firm says the stock faces a higher bar after rebounding in recent weeks and being up about 40 percent over the past six months. Microsoft has beaten earnings estimates in each of the last four quarters. Analysts expect revenues of 570 billion dollars and earnings of 216.7 billion dollars by 2029, which corresponds to 19.8 percent yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about 83 billion dollars from 133.7 billion dollars today.

Recent announcements from partners such as Bloomberg Law, Trellis, Wood Mackenzie, Resilinc and Tucuvi show Microsoft Copilot and Azure being embedded directly into legal, energy, healthcare and supply chain workflows. The main risk remains whether AI or cloud usage slows versus Microsoft's 175 billion to 190 billion dollar 2026 capex plans, which could squeeze free cash flow and margins. More cautious analysts were assuming Microsoft would reach about 508.6 billion dollars in revenue and 204.6 billion dollars in earnings by 2029, with a lower price to earnings ratio of 20.9 times. If Azure growth falls short, capacity limits persist or OpenAI news hits the backlog, the AI spending worry that sent shares down after the fiscal 2026 third quarter report could return.

stories.Headline: Federal privacy legislation in 2026: The 49 bills reshaping US data privacy law
stories.Summary:
By September 2026, lawmakers in the 119th Congress had introduced 49 distinct federal privacy proposals, according to the IAPP tracker cited by Captain Compliance. The proposals cover consumer privacy, artificial intelligence, children's data, employee surveillance, reproductive information, precise location data, financial information, connected vehicles, data brokers, automated decision-making and age verification. Several proposals have House and Senate companions, so the actual number of bill numbers is higher. Only two tracked proposals have become law so far: the TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed May 19, 2025, and the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act, signed September 5, 2025. Congress is debating three versions of comprehensive consumer privacy legislation at the same time.

The Online Privacy Act of 2026 was introduced March 19, 2026, and referred to three House committees, and it would create rights of access, correction, deletion and portability and establish a Digital Privacy Agency. Sen. Jerry Moran's Consumer Data Privacy and Security Act was introduced March 25, 2026, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and it would preempt covered state privacy laws and lacks a private right of action. The SECURE Data Act, H.R. 8413, would set a national framework, preempt covered state rules and also lacks a general private right of action. The disputes over state-law preemption and private rights of action remain unresolved. More than 20 states have enacted broad consumer privacy regimes, and the Future of Privacy Forum counted 21 comprehensive state laws when the SECURE Data Act was introduced in April 2026.

Industry groups including the Software & Information Industry Association have backed national uniformity, while California regulators and a coalition of attorneys general have taken the opposing view. Some narrower bills expressly preserve state laws, others expressly preempt them, and many do neither. Ideas once found mainly in comprehensive bills are moving into sector-specific measures, including data minimization, deletion rights, opt-outs, sensitive-data restrictions and limits on targeted advertising. Privacy and AI governance are increasingly overlapping compliance disciplines, with AI provisions appearing in consumer, employment and children's privacy bills. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the committee stage of the tracked proposals.

stories.Headline: Europe startups weigh relocation as AI regulation and funding gaps strain growth
stories.Summary:
Regulatory hurdles, funding shortages and gaps in workforce skills are pushing European startups to consider relocating, according to Tanuja Randery, the managing director for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Amazon Web Services. She spoke to Reuters on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, in an interview with the Reuters Global Markets Forum. She said the region risks a mass exit of its most promising new ventures. Europe has struggled to close the gap with the US and China in the AI race because of tighter regulations, energy constraints and concerns about data privacy. Randery said European businesses report spending as much as 40 cents of every euro on regulatory compliance instead of technology.

She cited an AWS survey of companies finding that nearly 4 in 10 European startups would consider leaving the region to scale, and among the fastest-growing ones the share is over half. She said startups are reconsidering locations because they want funding and support and are not getting enough funding in Europe. More than half of businesses in Europe use AI, but she said only one in five are clear about AI strategy, have an AI governance model and are invested in processes that would reshape operations. She added that inferencing, the stage where trained AI models are run to produce outputs for real-world use, is where European businesses need to invest.

Randery is responsible for the comments, which come from her interview with Reuters and from the AWS survey she cited. She said European businesses could reinvest the money spent on compliance into technology. She said Europe needs to go faster and that the choice is not progress versus safety, calling it an and rather than an or. The articles also cite the European Union's AI Act, widely seen as the world's most stringent AI regulatory framework, as a limit on Europe's efforts.

Severe energy and grid constraints are also stymying progress. Europe has produced few frontier AI models of its own and depends instead on companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Tech majors are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into frontier research and scaling AI infrastructure, while Europe's efforts have been limited. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the survey findings and Randery's comments.

stories.Headline: Using Machine Learning to Predict Microphysical Properties of Cloud Ice Crystals
stories.Summary:
Researchers developed a machine learning framework to predict the 3D microphysical properties of ice crystals from 2D images taken inside real clouds. The team, led by Ko, J., and others, published the work in JGR: Machine Learning & Computation. The study appeared in October 2026 through the Department of Energy Office of Science. The team first generated synthetic ice crystals using 3D modeling software and geometric parameters estimated from the Ice Cryo-Encapsulation Balloon campaign, known as ICEBall.

ICEBall was a 2021 field campaign run by the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Office of Science User Facility. Researchers used scanning electron microscopy to measure real ice crystal samples from the campaign to help build the synthetic crystals. They then trained machine learning models on the synthetic crystals to predict mass, surface area, and the number of spikes of individual crystals. On unseen synthetic images, the models accurately predicted these ice crystal properties.

The research was funded by the National Science Foundation through the Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics Science and Technology Center, or LEAP. Support also came from the DOE Atmospheric System Research program. The work drew on the State University of New York, Albany's Atmospheric Sciences Research Center Extreme Collaboration, Innovation, and Technology, or xCITE. The team also received computing support from the Derecho and Casper systems provided by the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research.

The study says representing clouds accurately in Earth system models is difficult because complex microphysical properties and processes govern cloud behavior. Ice clouds pose a particularly acute challenge because the shapes of ice crystals influence overall cloud behavior. The framework offers a way to estimate ice microphysical properties from in-cloud imagery, which the study says will enable downstream constraints on microphysical parameterizations, such as the relationship between mass and size. The findings are expected to help improve how clouds are represented in computer models of the Earth's atmosphere.

stories.Headline: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Bob McGrew, a former research executive at OpenAI, has been quietly building an AI manufacturing startup called Arda, the company revealed in an exclusive interview with CNBC on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Arda has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, with the round led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures. McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before leaving in a 2024 wave of high-profile exits. His co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked at Google and Meta, along with former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick.

Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing, and McGrew described it as a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers. He said a design change can take a day to retrain a human but three to six months to change the automation, and Arda's product lets engineers build assembly lines much faster. The company uses a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril, and McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap.

Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal, who led the recent funding round and met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir, said manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry and $3 trillion in the U.S. alone. He said the price is steep today but the long-term opportunity is very high, and he believes Arda will capture a significant portion of that market. McGrew said that if a design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly. He also said no one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S., and that building one there would bring American jobs rather than take them away.

The launch comes as the AI industry faces pressure to prove its value beyond chatbots and code generation, and as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing. McGrew said he stayed at OpenAI through the November 2023 weekend when CEO Sam Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired, because he wanted to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the last key breakthrough left before AGI. He said OpenAI is an amazing place and that he remembers being in rooms with Altman, Dario Amodei and Ilya Sutskever talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you. Arda's success will depend on whether it can deliver real results in actual manufacturing environments, and the next 12 months will reveal whether its manufacturing vision can match its billion-dollar ambitions.

stories.Headline: BULL SAS: Bull and CRA join forces to build the Czech AI Gigafactory for Central and Eastern Europe
stories.Summary:
On 21 October 2026, Bull and České Radiokomunikace (CRA) signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding to combine their expertise and develop a sovereign AI offering for the Czech Republic and Central and Eastern Europe. The agreement was announced in Paris and Prague. It is the first industrial agreement announced under the bilateral strategic cooperation agreement on AI and digital technology signed by Anne Le Hénanff, Minister Delegate for Artificial Intelligence of the French Republic, and Karel Havlíček, Minister of Industry and Trade of the Czech Republic. The partnership strengthens the consortium led by CRA in its candidacy under the European AI Gigafactories programme.

The Czech AI Gigafactory initiative is open to companies from nine Central and Eastern European countries under the Prague declaration: the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Croatia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovenia and Romania. The consortium aims to maximise the share of European technologies across its infrastructure and AI stack. Bull's manufacturing capabilities in the Czech Republic and France, in partnership with Foxconn, could enable the consortium to build the Gigafactory's computing servers in both countries, with the ambition to integrate European chips as they become available. The open-source-based BullSequana AI platform, developed by teams in Prague, Brno and France, will let organisations develop and deploy AI applications, supported by more than 200 DataSentics AI engineers in the Czech Republic. Bull also intends to reserve Gigafactory capacity for its own clients.

Emmanuel Le Roux, CEO of Bull, said AI Gigafactories are where the company's hardware, AI software and expertise in real-world AI applications come together. He said joining the Czech consortium is an important step in Bull's European AI strategy and strengthens Czech-French cooperation, building on the 200 DataSentics engineers in Prague and Brno. He described the kind of AI Bull wants to build in Europe as open, sustainable and sovereign, giving organisations greater control over their technology and data. Miloš Mastník, CEO of CRA, said the ambition is to build an ecosystem in the Czech Republic that combines computing infrastructure with the development and practical use of artificial intelligence. He said the Memorandum with Bull opens opportunities for cooperation in hardware and software, the two key components of an AI Gigafactory, and that international and Czech companies, public administrations and researchers should be able to develop their own AI solutions there, helping the Czech Republic become a major centre for artificial intelligence in Europe.

AI Gigafactories are intended to strengthen Europe's resilience and capacity to develop and deploy advanced AI at scale, providing computing infrastructure, services and expertise to companies, research organisations and public administrations while helping Europe retain greater control over its data, technologies and strategic AI capabilities. Bull brings end-to-end AI capabilities to the consortium, and its experience in energy efficient supercomputing includes Direct Liquid Cooling and workload-level energy monitoring, while the BullSequana AI platform routes routine tasks to right-sized open models to reduce cost and energy consumption. Bull's dual role as technology provider and future user gives it a direct interest in the Gigafactory's utilisation and long-term success. CRA operates eight data centres and its own fibre-optic backbone network, already provides GPU computing capacity in the Czech Republic, and is developing the AIGF CZ project for Central and Eastern Europe as part of the European AI Gigafactory initiative.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence-enabled triage tools may reflect human biases : Newsroom
stories.Summary:
UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers published a study in npj Digital Medicine on October 20, 2026, finding that artificial intelligence-driven triage tools used in emergency departments may be susceptible to the same clinical stigmas as human assessments. The team analyzed patient records from emergency departments at Stanford Medicine in California and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Massachusetts. They paired patients with similar initial condition severity levels and asked three open-source AI large language models to predict which patients were more likely to deteriorate and who should be prioritized for care. Before demographic, social, or potentially stigmatizing information was added, all three models identified higher-risk patients at rates well above chance.

Researchers then added different types of information to patient records, including mental health and substance use history, age, and patterns of emergency department use, and evaluated how the models' decisions changed. They compared neutral language with stigmatizing language, such as "established patient with multiple chronic conditions" versus "17 visits in the past 12 months," and "opioid use disorder, on maintenance therapy" versus "active IV drug use, heroin, last use today." Details associated with clinical stigma often influenced how the AI systems prioritized patients, and in some cases information unrelated to a patient's immediate medical condition caused the models to lower the priority of patients who later experienced serious deterioration. Some of the strongest effects appeared when records described patients as frequent emergency department users or included a history of psychiatric emergencies, and in some instances nearly 10% of patients were incorrectly downgraded after stigmatizing information was added. Age also influenced some decisions, though the researchers believe those effects likely reflected the greater medical risks often associated with older age rather than age-related bias.

First author Philip Jarrett, an Assistant Professor of Emergency Medicine, said wording matters because AI models process the words used to describe patients, and stigmatizing language can steer clinicians away from the patients who need care most. He said the study is part of a broader research program on how clinical information should be presented to AI so it can safely help prioritize emergency patients competing for limited resources. Senior author Andrew Jamieson, an Assistant Professor in the Lyda Hill Department of Bioinformatics, said a single added detail sometimes shifted a model's priority away from the patient who later deteriorated. Jarrett said one of the main takeaways is that bias varies by model, so each AI tool should be tested against real patient outcomes before use.

The authors concluded that as hospitals increasingly explore using AI to help prioritize care, the way patient information is documented could influence whether these systems make fair and accurate decisions. Jarrett said the next step of the research is to develop models that predict clinical deterioration in the emergency department based on both structured data and clinical text. Jamieson said AI is expanding what can be done with complex information and that a big part of the work is learning what shapes the systems' answers, how those answers vary, and what that means in clinical practice. The study was supported by institutional funds from the UT Southwestern Medical Center Office of the President and has also received grant funding from the National Foundation of Emergency Medicine for follow-up research.

stories.Headline: Clover School District pauses student use of most AI platforms
stories.Summary:
Clover School District in South Carolina began blocking student access to most artificial intelligence tools on district-issued devices on Oct. 21, 2026, according to a message sent to families. The district's Technology team started blocking publicly available AI platforms to the best of its ability that day. Only SchoolAI remains available to students during the temporary pause announced Wednesday. District officials said the pause is meant to strengthen expectations for responsible AI use, better protect student information, and give schools time to establish consistent guidelines for classrooms.

The restrictions are not permanent, and the district said its technology filters cannot guarantee that every AI resource will be blocked. During the pause, teachers are asked to plan classroom activities involving AI around SchoolAI and not direct students to other AI platforms. SchoolAI is available through ClassLink to middle and high school teachers and students, as well as elementary school teachers. Elementary students will not have access to SchoolAI.

The district's Technology team is responsible for blocking access to the public AI platforms. District innovation coaches will provide teachers with additional information about accessing SchoolAI, incorporating it into instruction, and obtaining support. District officials said the pause is intended to strengthen expectations for responsible AI use and protect student information. The district said it will share more information about its next steps and opportunities for staff to participate as it continues developing its approach to AI in schools.

The change was announced as a temporary pause, and the district said it will share more information about next steps as it develops its approach. Teachers are being directed to use SchoolAI for classroom instruction during the pause. Innovation coaches will give teachers information on using SchoolAI in instruction and getting support. The district said it will share opportunities for staff to participate as it continues developing its approach to AI in schools.
