stories.Headline: The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations
stories.Summary:
Check Point Research published a report on October 20, 2026, warning that antidetect browsers powered by AI are being used for online fraud and influence operations. These browsers hide a user's digital identity, letting one operator run thousands of separate accounts on platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram and YouTube without being caught. The report names three main tools, Kameleo, AdsPower and MultiLogin, and says they have been referenced on underground forums and criminal marketplaces. Confirmed uses include taking over accounts with stolen session cookies, testing stolen card details, filing fraudulent loan applications and creating fake accounts to generate advertising revenue.

The report says these tools now include AI features, from built-in automation templates to a dedicated MCP server that feeds content generated by large language models directly into prepared account profiles at machine speed. It says running a large-scale social media operation now needs only a credit card instead of a technical team. AdsPower, which began in China and is localized into more than 20 languages, spoofs more than 20 configurable parameters per profile and advertises a 99.2% ban avoidance rate. The report also cites Anthropic's September 2026 Threat Intelligence Report, which described attackers using antidetect browsers with residential proxies, automated CAPTCHA solving and identity-verification bypass tools to create many verified accounts for fraud.

The report says the companies behind these browsers present them as legitimate platforms for digital marketing, e-commerce and privacy protection. It says Kameleo's engineering team published a guide on automating Facebook likes across many accounts, and that Kameleo appears in posts on Russian-language hacking forums, including one advertising a phishing kit that targets Google, Microsoft, Facebook and financial platforms. Meta's most recent transparency reporting flagged coordinated fake activity as a growing concern, naming Russia, Iran and China as the three leading sources globally. The report says platforms mainly detect coordinated activity at the account and behavioral layer, while antidetect browsers run below the surface and stay undetected.

TechRadar reported on the findings on October 21, 2026, in an article by Sead Fadilpašić saying the browsers are making scams, fraud and influence operations harder to spot. The report says the risk is growing because these accounts can pass identity checks, build normal-looking activity histories and appear harmless during transactions, so fraud systems often spot them only after the damage is done. It notes the concern is greater ahead of elections, when such accounts could be used to coordinate influence operations. The articles do not say what happens next beyond describing the threat and the tools involved.

Articles.Title: The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations

stories.Headline: RBC Weighs Blocking Meta's AI Agent Muse, CEO McKay Says
stories.Summary:
Dave McKay, the president and chief executive of Royal Bank of Canada, said he is considering blocking Meta Platforms Inc.'s artificial intelligence agent Muse from the bank's customer information. He made the comment on Bloomberg Surveillance in an interview reported on 20 October 2026. McKay said the bank has to protect the consumer and that the organization is liable. The agent is described in the report as popular.

The step under consideration would stop Muse from reaching RBC customer data. McKay framed the issue as a matter of consumer protection and of the bank's own liability as an organization. The report gives no date for a decision and no details of how a block would work. It also gives no figures on how many customers or accounts could be affected.

McKay is the person responsible for the bank's position, as president and chief executive, and he set out his reasoning in the interview. He said, in paraphrase, that protecting the consumer comes first and that the bank carries liability for that protection. The articles do not say whether Meta has responded or been asked about the plan. They also do not say whether other banks are weighing similar moves.

The articles give little beyond McKay's comment, so what happens next is not yet known. It is not clear when RBC might decide or what a block would mean for customers who use Muse. Meta has not commented in the reports, and no regulator is named. More to follow.

stories.Headline: County College of Morris accepting applications for paid AI and data science apprenticeship
stories.Summary:
County College of Morris is accepting applications through Nov. 2 for its artificial intelligence and data science apprenticeship program. The program is open to CCM students and adult learners who live in New Jersey and want careers in artificial intelligence, machine learning and data science. It combines classroom instruction with hands-on training from industry professionals. Applications must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. Monday, Nov. 2, 2026.

Participants must complete 30 college credits and 2,000 hours of paid, on-the-job training. They then earn a certificate in AI and Data Science from CCM and a Registered Apprenticeship Certificate of Completion from the New Jersey Department of Labor. Tuition and fees toward the certificate may be covered for eligible participants. Credits can also be applied toward a 60-credit associate degree at CCM, with the chance to transfer to a four-year university for a bachelor's degree.

Nancy Binowski, professor of AI and Data Science at CCM, said artificial intelligence and data science are reshaping the global economy at an unprecedented pace. She said the earn-and-learn model gives students real-world experience in an in-demand field. She said employers also get a chance to develop emerging talent and apply AI and data science solutions to business needs. The program also gives employers a way to train emerging professionals and help them build workplace skills.

With support from the New Jersey Community College Consortium for Workforce and Economic Development, CCM was selected as one of two community colleges in New Jersey to help deliver the state's first U.S. Department of Labor-registered AI and Data Science Apprenticeship. The initiative is meant to prepare workers for careers in artificial intelligence and data science across many industries. Employers interested in partnering can email AIApprenticeship@ccm.edu or call 973-328-5703. More to follow.

stories.Headline: MU: AI-driven memory demand is met with expanding DRAM, HBM, NAND and storage roadmaps
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology outlined a technology and product roadmap on October 21, 2026, during its technology and product leadership webinar. President and Chief Technology and Products Officer Scott DeBoer said AI is changing memory from a supporting component into a central constraint on system performance, capacity and cost per token. The roadmap covers next-generation DRAM, high-bandwidth memory, NAND and advanced packaging. Micron said AI is driving demand across training, inference, agents and physical AI.

The plan includes 1-delta DRAM volume production in the second half of 2027, with a mid-20% improvement in bit density. Micron is in high-volume production of HBM4 and is developing custom HBM, HBM4E and vertical HBM. Generation 11 NAND is expected to ramp in the second half of 2027, more than double bit density versus Generation 9, target 1.5 times the I/O speed and use more than 400 layers. LPDDR6 is expected to provide 35% better power performance than LPDDR5, and DDR6 is described as offering twice the bandwidth of DDR5.

DeBoer said Micron aims to advance memory, storage and compute together through higher bandwidth, larger capacities, better power efficiency and closer collaboration with customers. He said the company has confidence in several more generations of planar DRAM scaling before 3D DRAM, and that 3D DRAM timing will depend on cost, complexity and device performance. He said hybrid bonding is necessary as interconnect pitches tighten, citing bandwidth and thermal benefits. He also said Micron does not expect memory supply to come into balance over the next two years.

Micron said it is using AI internally to speed development, citing a data center controller design that moved from silicon to tape-out in half the time of the prior generation. The company pointed to longer-term investments, including expanded Micron Ventures activity, work at Albany NanoTech and a previously announced $10 billion, 10-year commitment to Micron Research Labs. DeBoer said Micron is collaborating with partners ranging from startup Liqid to Meta, and the two companies recently published a white paper on optimizing LPDDR6 for data centers. He said memory configurations will vary across training, inference, edge and rack-scale deployments, but more memory content and bandwidth improve system performance.

stories.Headline: Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg launched Enterprise MCP for its Data Licence Plus service on October 20, 2026. The system connects Bloomberg data to clients' artificial intelligence applications through a standardised interface covering more than 100 million securities and over 50,000 fields. It combines metadata on data fields with semantic search tools and workflow-specific functions, allowing users to request information in natural language instead of relying on field codes or manual identifier matching. The service includes entity resolution tools designed to map names, tickers or descriptions to the correct instrument and its links to the issuing company.

The service provides details including what a data field represents, how it was calculated, when it applies, and qualifiers such as currency, exchange, price type, period and date. Bloomberg hosts and manages the access layer, while clients retain control over the AI agents and applications connected to it, including the models, prompts and instructions used in their workflows. Bloomberg validates a firm's entitlements before returning data in response to an agent request under standard Data Licence rights. Requests are resolved against Bloomberg's Operational Datastore, while tool-level limits cap the number of securities and fields returned in a single call. The initial release includes workflow skills covering point-in-time universe retrieval, corporate action adjustment and revision history, plus tools to identify outliers in a group of tickers, review trades that breach accepted price deviation thresholds, and assess securities and trades for possible sanctions exposure.

Tony McManus, Global Head of Enterprise Data and Indices at Bloomberg, said the bottleneck facing financial institutions has shifted from model capability to data readiness. He said agents that reason well still cannot answer a basic question about a position because the data reaching them carries no indication of what it actually represents. On its own, a last price does not say what currency it is in or what kind of price it is. McManus said connections were never the hard part, readiness is, and that is what Bloomberg built Enterprise MCP to solve.

The launch comes as data providers, banks and financial software firms race to position themselves in the growing market for AI tools in regulated industries. Bloomberg said its engineers have been involved in proposals related to governance controls within the Model Context Protocol and in methods that allow servers to present tailored toolsets to different clients. It added that it leads the MCP Financial Services Interest Group and holds seats on the board and Technical Committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, which oversees the protocol as an open standard. Clients can license specific content domains under standard Bloomberg Data Licence rights.

stories.Headline: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
stories.Summary:
Google said Tuesday it is upgrading its Gemini AI assistant in vehicles with a feature called Personal Intelligence. The feature can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand a user’s preferences, activities, and past experiences. It launches in Android Auto starting today and will expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini in Android Auto last November, while Personal Intelligence rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

Drivers must opt in for Personal Intelligence to work, and they can turn it off at any time and choose which apps to connect. Once enabled, a driver heading to the airport may be alerted that a flight on their calendar is delayed. A user can ask for a flight gate and then ask if the flight is still on time, and Gemini will answer both questions at once. The feature also lets users say things like “Take me to my doctor’s appointment” or “Find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” On Android Automotive, personalized responses will only be shared when the user’s phone is connected in the car.

Google said users retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The company described the upgrade as connecting the dots across users’ Google apps. If a user does not enable Personal Intelligence, navigation, music, calls, and questions still work in the car, but answers will not be tailored to them. Google said the feature will come to Android Auto automatically if it was already enabled for the Gemini app on a phone.

Separately, the Japanese company Kokusai Chotatsu Joho said its AI gateway FastMetal began offering Google’s large language model Gemini 4 Argon on October 14, 2026. Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, as the first model in the Gemini 4 generation, aimed at practical coding, corporate intellectual work, and cyber defense. FastMetal prices it at 357.4 yen per million input tokens and 1,787 yen per million output tokens, before tax, with a context length of 1,048,576 tokens. The service supports yen payments, prepaid credit, credit cards, bank transfers, and qualified invoices, and it can read images and PDFs.

stories.Headline: Toku launches Makimoto Flows, a visual builder for speech AI pipelines, taking its open-source initiative beyond transcription
stories.Summary:
Toku Ltd., a Singapore-headquartered AI customer experience platform listed on SGX, launched Makimoto Flows on 21 October 2026. Flows is a visual builder inside the company's open-source conversational AI initiative, and it lets developers assemble speech AI pipelines block by block and test each stage on a recorded call. The tool is live at makimoto.ai. On the canvas, developers connect blocks and test each step on its own. The Transcribe block turns audio into text using Kawa, the Summarise block generates a topic and short summary from the transcript, and the Tags block sorts each call into seven categories, including customer sentiment.

Every block runs in Singapore, so audio, transcripts and analysis stay in the country. A Chained Analysis starter template links the blocks in one click, and developers can change any block and rerun it to compare results. Each block maps to a Makimoto API endpoint, and any flow can be exported as ready-to-run Python code for uses such as call recaps and call triage. Thomas Laboulle, founder and CEO at Toku, said developers should control how their voice AI works, from the models they use to the way each stage connects. He said Flows puts the orchestration layer in front of them, so they can build a pipeline, run a recorded call through it and see what each step produces before anything reaches customers.

He added that models will keep changing, and the ability to compose them and know where they run is what lasts. Flows builds on the composable architecture Toku set out when it introduced Makimoto in April 2026 and takes the initiative beyond transcription. Kawa was released on schedule on 1 July 2026 and set up the transcription layer through a Singapore-hosted API, and summarisation and tagging endpoints followed in September. Next, Makimoto plans to add audio preparation blocks, starting with noise filtering. Developers can create a free account at makimoto.ai, and each account includes 1,000 free minutes.

stories.Headline: Anthropic, Google, ByteDance & Tencent Join the Fray: Why Tech Giants Are Collectively Flocking to AI-Powered Drug Discovery
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, Google, ByteDance and Tencent have all moved into AI-powered drug discovery, according to a 36Kr report published on October 20, 2026. Anthropic has started building physical wet labs and is recruiting biochemistry talent. Google's Isomorphic Labs keeps upgrading the AlphaFold protein structure prediction model, and its latest valuation reached 40 to 50 billion US dollars. ByteDance spun off its AI pharmaceutical company Anew Labs, which raised 290 million US dollars in a first round at a post-investment valuation of about 1.5 billion US dollars.

The article says AI compresses drug discovery time by 30 to 50 percent, and that AI-discovered molecules reach 80 to 90 percent success in Phase I trials against a historical average of 52 percent. More than 170 AI drug projects worldwide have entered clinical stages, and 7 AI drugs have entered or completed Phase III trials. Isomorphic Labs' IsoDDE engine is said to cut a search of 10^60 chemical spaces from several years to several days. Insilico Medicine's Rentosertib, found with AI help, has entered Phase III trials for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, predicted that AI could overcome most serious diseases in the next 5 to 10 years. Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind has said the best use of AI is to improve human health, and he shared half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold. The US FDA said digital transformation will not change existing CGMP requirements and that quality oversight cannot be transferred because of AI. No AI drug has yet passed regulatory approval and reached the market.

The 36Kr article notes that AI mainly changes the upstream discovery stage, which accounts for only 38 percent of costs, while 62 percent goes to clinical trials and approval. It names high-quality data as the biggest bottleneck, since failed molecule data held by drug companies and CROs is rarely made public. Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta plan to invest 1.8 billion US dollars in a next-generation biological AI model and open data infrastructure. A separate Yahoo Finance article says Tencent joined ByteDance and Alibaba in placing large 2026 orders for Nvidia high-end AI chips, with combined orders exceeding Nvidia's planned output.

stories.Headline: How Is NVIDIA Expanding AI-Powered Telecom Networks Following T-Mobile’s First AI-RAN Call?
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA announced at its GTC Berlin event that T-Mobile US completed what the companies described as the world's first AI Radio Access Network call on a commercial mobile network. The demonstration took place in Bellevue, Washington, with NVIDIA and Nokia. It used commercial NVIDIA Aerial RAN Computer servers, Nokia's CUDA-accelerated radio access network software and massive MIMO radio equipment. The system ran on an existing standalone 5G core network and used a commercially available smartphone.

AI-RAN combines artificial intelligence with the radio access network infrastructure that connects mobile devices to telecom networks. NVIDIA's ARC platform is designed to provide computing for both radio access functions and AI applications on shared infrastructure. BT plans live network trials in Birmingham, England, during 2027, and Deutsche Telekom has validated the platform in labs in Bonn, Germany, and Oulu, Finland, with field trials planned for 2027. Elisa completed what Nokia and NVIDIA described as Europe's first AI-RAN field trial, running voice, mobile data and video analytics on a single ARC platform.

NVIDIA said nine operators across Europe, the Middle East and Africa are developing or expanding infrastructure based on its technology. NVIDIA unveiled two more ARC configurations, MGX 2U and MGX 4U, using RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with x86 or NVIDIA Vera CPU options. Dell Technologies, Quanta Cloud Technology and Supermicro are expected to offer servers for the platform. Nokia is putting the Nemotron family of open AI models into its Autonomous Networks Suite, and Cisco is integrating fine-tuned versions into its Crosswork AI platform.

Tata Consultancy Services, BT and NTT DATA are also adopting Nemotron models to build AI agents for telecom operations. The announcements extend NVIDIA's role beyond conventional computing hardware into radio access networks and network automation software. Several announced projects remain at the laboratory validation or trial stage, and the companies have not disclosed comprehensive financial terms or revenue expectations. Further deployments and testing will provide more information about operational performance and commercial applications.

stories.Headline: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
stories.Summary:
SpaceX reported third quarter revenue of $14.6 billion on Tuesday, a 161 percent increase from the same period a year earlier. The company earned $4.40 billion in net income, turning around from a loss of $1.05 billion a year ago. Its artificial intelligence business, renamed Super Intelligence, generated $7.5 billion in revenue and $431 million in profit. That profit would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one time stock based compensation expenses tied to the Cursor acquisition. The AI unit includes the Cursor coding tool, the Grok bot, and a neocloud business with 1.7 gigawatts of compute.

The results show AI now makes up 52 percent of SpaceX income. The connectivity segment, which includes Starlink, reported $5.2 billion in revenue, up 69 percent from a year earlier, and Starlink reached 13.6 million consumers. Total capital expenditures were $19.6 billion, and Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter. Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion. SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million in the first nine months of the year.

Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, at the Colossus II data center site. He said the constraint on deploying super intelligence is more in power, cooling, and infrastructure than in chips, and he compared SpaceX engineers to the New York Yankees playing in Little League. Musk said turbine makers face 12 to 18 month delays for metal blades and vanes, so SpaceX is using its metal casting capabilities to make those parts. He also said the next Starship test flight, expected in November, would attempt to recover both the first stage booster and the second stage.

SpaceX shares jumped nearly 4 percent in after hours trading to about $153.30, and the company has a valuation of nearly $1.95 trillion. This was the company’s second ever quarterly financial disclosure since it went public in June. Musk predicted SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion. The earnings release came a day after Musk vowed to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year, a pledge that could total nearly $11 billion based on about 73 million people under age 18.

stories.Headline: KAIST develops AI that sees through clouds to restore satellite imagery
stories.Summary:
KAIST announced on October 20 that a research team led by Professor Moon-Chul Kim of the School of Electrical Engineering, with researcher Jung-Hyuk Do of the Information and Electronics Research Institute, developed an AI model called GeoCore-9B. The model can restore satellite images obscured by clouds and convert synthetic aperture radar images into natural-looking optical photographs. The team built the model from scratch using satellite data rather than adapting an existing general-purpose image-generation AI. The research was accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026, and the paper was released on August 3 on the preprint server arXiv.

GeoCore-9B has about 9 billion parameters and was trained on 10 million pairs of satellite images from around the world, along with descriptive captions. The model also learned latitude, longitude, and ground sampling distance, which specifies how large an area one pixel represents on the ground. This lets the AI determine the real-world scale of buildings, roads, and industrial facilities. The team applied a technique called geospatial semantic alignment, which helps the model learn spatial characteristics such as road connectivity and farmland boundaries without increasing computational cost during image generation. For specialized tasks like cloud removal and radar image conversion, the team used the LoRA approach, which keeps the core model intact and trains only small additional components.

Professor Kim said that by training the model on both the capture location of satellite images and the actual scale of the terrain, the team enabled a single AI to perform multiple tasks such as cloud removal and image conversion. He said the team expects this to broaden the use of satellite data that was previously difficult to exploit due to weather or imaging methods, and to help assess disaster situations and monitor changes in forests and cities. In experiments using publicly available satellite data, GeoCore-9B outperformed existing specialized AI models on key metrics measuring brightness, color, and structural similarity in cloud-obscured image restoration. In tests converting radar imagery to optical images, it achieved top scores on some metrics evaluating image quality and fine structural detail.

The technology is expected to support image analysis in regions where cloud cover hampers observation, as well as visualization of radar data. It could be applied to disaster monitoring, including wildfires, floods, and landslides, and to tracking environmental changes such as deforestation and urban expansion. However, its effectiveness in actual disaster response and national territory surveillance will require further verification. The team plans to expand validation across a wider range of satellite sensors and regions, and to extend applied research into defense-related surveillance, reconnaissance, and battlefield situation analysis.

stories.Headline: Walmart launches tools for AI agents to shop for customers
stories.Summary:
Walmart on Wednesday unveiled tools that let artificial intelligence agents shop on behalf of its customers. The company said it would launch Agent Profiles within the next month. Customers will be able to register each AI assistant they use as a separate profile within their Walmart account. Purchases made by an agent will then appear apart from the customer's own. Walmart compared the arrangement to adding an authorized user to a credit card.

The tools require customers to register each AI assistant as its own profile, and they can delete a profile at any time. Customers can require approval for every purchase or let an agent buy on its own up to a spending limit they set, such as $50, $100 or $200. The move contrasts with rival Amazon, the largest US online retailer, which blocks third-party shopping agents while promoting its own AI tools such as Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me. Last month Amazon blocked Meta's Muse from its site, with users shown a notice saying unauthorized AI agents violate Amazon's conditions of use. Amazon sued Perplexity in November 2025, accusing the startup of using its Comet browser agent to covertly make purchases on its marketplace.

Walmart is responsible for the new profiles, and it compared the arrangement to adding an authorized user to a credit card. Anthropic on Wednesday released a preview of Claude Duet, an agent that works in the background across users' connected apps and can make online purchases with their approval. OpenAI launched its own always-on agents, called Dots, last month. Meta launched Muse in September and has made it available only in the United States and Canada, where it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, according to an analysis of third-party data by Sensor Tower.

The context is heavy investment in AI agents, which much of the industry sees as the next phase of the AI boom that followed the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. Tech companies including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta are investing heavily in agents. AI agents are programs that can carry out multi-step tasks on a user's behalf, such as searching for products, comparing prices and completing a purchase, rather than only answering questions as chatbots do. Amazon has also moved to restrict agents from Google and OpenAI.

stories.Headline: Tod Machover’s new symphony plays with AI while reflecting on democracy
stories.Summary:
Composer Tod Machover's new symphony "already and not yet" will have its world premiere with the Boston Symphony Orchestra on Thursday, October 22, 2026. The performances run October 22 to 24 at Boston's Symphony Hall. Conductor Kent Nagano, a longtime collaborator of Machover's, will lead the orchestra. The piece was commissioned by the Boston Symphony Orchestra and supported by the New Works Fund of the Massachusetts Cultural Council.

The symphony has three movements that trace stages of democracy. The first, "Smash Up," has strings and winds crowded out by what Machover calls oppressive sounds of brass, percussion, and electronics. The second, "Wake Up," is a time to reflect and regroup, and it gradually builds a thriving melodic presence. The third, "Stand Up," involves vigorous interplay among all the musicians, who help establish a new balance between individuality and community. A "Live AI" system built at the MIT Media Lab, plus electronics from Machover's studio, shapes the piece, with the AI underscoring each player in the second movement and building sonic bridges in the third.

Machover, the Muriel R. Cooper Professor of Music and Media and faculty director at the MIT Media Lab, wrote the music, and the musicians create the live sound. The AI system analyzes features in that sound and works with the material as it is performed, sometimes acting like an accompanist and sometimes answering the orchestra in call-and-response sections. Machover credits two PhD candidates in his Media Lab group: Manaswi Mishra, who designed and built the AI systems, and Ana Schon, who will handle sound mixing in Symphony Hall. Machover said he condemns commercial uses of generative AI in music, calling prompt-based song creation the opposite of creativity.

The performances are coordinated with the MIT Media Lab's 40th anniversary celebrations this week, and Machover has been a member of the lab since it opened. He said the piece is in many ways an homage to the lab and its spirit of invention. Machover has explored AI and technology in music for decades, including hyperinstruments played by cellist Yo-Yo Ma, and his 2010 opera "Death and the Powers" was a Pulitzer Prize finalist. His next "City Symphony," underway in Seoul, South Korea, is scheduled to premiere in September 2027.

stories.Headline: AI-Generated Fake Doctors Flood YouTube in Korea - Seoul Economic Daily
stories.Summary:
Data released by Rep. Park Yong-gap of the Democratic Party of Korea at a parliamentary audit on the 20th of October, 2026, showed that 42 of the top 100 YouTube videos on senior health posted in April were made with generative AI. Of those 42, 24 impersonated doctors or other medical professionals, while only six of the 100 videos featured a genuine expert. The Korea Health Promotion Institute submitted the data to Park, a member of the National Assembly's Health and Welfare Committee. The fake videos used white coats, specialist titles and staged hospital scenes to win trust, and some carried no disclosure that AI had been used.

The videos spread claims without medical grounds, such as that warm water works better than stomach medicine and that frozen blueberries cure diabetes. The institute found that AI-generated videos were seven times more likely to contain false information than videos with real experts. According to the Korea Press Foundation, more than 50 percent of people aged 70 and over watch online video, and institute data shows 45.4 percent of people in their 60s search for health information at least once a week. The institute can recommend voluntary corrections over harmful health information but has never actually requested that a video be deleted.

After Park raised the issue, Google Korea reviewed 100 videos across 51 channels, shut down 10 channels that violated its guidelines, removed 31 videos, added labels to 13 videos that had no AI disclosure and suspended monetization for 10 videos across five channels. YouTube has also tightened monetization limits since July on low-quality videos mass-produced with AI, including content where AI avatars modeled on real people give medical, financial or legal advice. Park said that as more older people get health information through platforms such as YouTube, there is a risk they will worsen their conditions through incorrect information. He called for a consultative body of public institutions, platforms and medical experts to conduct regular inspections and actively block harmful videos.

The articles also describe the rise of AI fake doctors as a money issue. In March, a YouTube channel that used AI to mimic the voice of professor Lee Cook-jong drew 40,000 subscribers in just one week, and in June authorities caught a company that used an AI doctor in advertising to sell ordinary food products as a miracle anti-aging remedy, with revenue of 8.1 billion won, about $5.6 million. The measures so far mainly limit advertising revenue, which prompts arguments that continuous oversight is needed to stop the circulation of false health information itself. The articles do not say what further action will follow.

Articles.Title: AI-Generated Fake Doctors Flood YouTube in Korea - Seoul Economic Daily
AI-Made Fake Doctors Flood Senior Health Videos on YouTube - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Everlaw Survey: In-House Legal Teams Are Using AI to Cut Law Firm Spend and 81% Expect Outcome-Based Pricing to Eclipse the Billable Hour Within Five Years - New Castle News
stories.Summary:
Everlaw, an AI litigation and investigations platform based in Oakland, California, released a survey on October 20, 2026, about how corporate legal departments use generative AI. The survey of 300 U.S. in-house legal professionals was conducted with Wakefield Research between June 26 and July 30, 2026. It found that 86 percent of in-house teams now use generative AI for legal work. According to the report, 54 percent of respondents whose departments use outside counsel say AI has already reduced the volume of work sent to law firms.

The survey reports that 81 percent of respondents expect outcome-based pricing to eclipse the billable hour within five years, including 47 percent who expect it within three years and 17 percent within 12 months. Among those who engage law firms, 62 percent expect clear disclosure of AI use, 61 percent expect measurable gains in efficiency or outcomes, and 60 percent expect lower fees or fewer billed hours when AI is used. Fifty-seven percent expect flat or fixed fees to be the most widely adopted alternative arrangement. The report also says 92 percent of respondents whose teams use generative AI report AI-related savings from outside counsel, with 13 percent describing the savings as significant and 56 percent as moderate.

Gloria Lee, Chief Legal Officer at Everlaw, said AI rebalances the relationship between in-house teams and their law firms. She said in-house teams can take control of certain types of work and act as strategic advisers on high-value challenges. Lee also said in-house teams have the motivation, which is cost savings, and the power, because they can already reduce their dependence on outside firms, to drive the shift to outcome-based billing. On risk, she said the erosion of legal skills is not something individuals can solve alone, and that law firms, clients, law schools and legal tech vendors all have a role in building training models.

The report also covers quality and risk. Seventy percent of those using or testing generative AI say it has improved accuracy and consistency in legal work. Respondents were more concerned about errors and misalignment, at 80 percent, and non-lawyers relying on generative AI for legal guidance, at 72 percent, than about other risks. One third have encountered AI-hallucinated evidence or case law in litigation, including 17 percent from opposing counsel and 12 percent from their own teams. Respondents still expect to pay law firms for judgment and expertise, with 56 percent saying clients should primarily pay outside counsel for business and commercial insight.

Articles.Title: Everlaw Survey: In-House Legal Teams Are Using AI to Cut Law Firm Spend and 81% Expect Outcome-Based Pricing to Eclipse the Billable Hour Within Five Years - New Castle News

stories.Headline: DC Council targets deceptive AI in real estate listings with proposed bill
stories.Summary:
A new bill in the DC Council targets deceptive AI in real estate listings. Councilmember Christina Henderson recently proposed the bill, and Councilmembers Matthew Frumin, Brianne K. Nadeau, Anita Bonds, Trayon White Sr., Janeese Lewis George, and Zachary Parker co-introduced it. The bill responds to listings with AI-enhanced descriptions and pictures that do not match the property in person. Real estate agent Stephanie Hill described a home advertised as completely renovated that was anything but when she arrived. If passed, the bill would require listing agents to disclose if images are digitally altered.

It would also require agents to include unedited images and a written description of the differences. Henderson said some examples involved a unit or room advertised as having a window when there was no window. She noted that DC is a transient city, and sometimes people sign leases without having seen the property. Hill said AI is a great tool for new ideas but that there needs to be a balance so facts are not overexaggerated. She said enhancements draw people in through emotion but let them down once they arrive, which serves neither seller nor buyer.

Her brokerage has a policy stating AI must not be used to alter the apparent demographics of a neighborhood, building, or street scene. The National Association of Realtors also created a template that brokerages can use to set their AI policy. The articles do not say what happens next with the bill. For people looking to buy or rent, the articles suggest reviewing and comparing a new listing with its previous listing. They also suggest verifying images with agents before appointments and requesting unedited photos.

Articles.Title: DC Council targets deceptive AI in real estate listings with proposed bill

stories.Headline: County Council passes law to regulate AI in Allegheny political ads
stories.Summary:
Allegheny County Council voted unanimously on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, to require candidates for county elected office to disclose the use of artificial intelligence in certain campaign materials. The legislation was sponsored by Councilman Dan Grzybek, D-Bethel Park, and at-large Councilman Alex Rose, I-Squirrel Hill. It advanced unanimously out of council's Government Reform Committee on Wednesday. The vote took place at the Allegheny County Courthouse.

Beginning in January, candidates seeking county elected office must label AI-generated or AI-altered political advertising. Failure to do so could result in fines or jail time. The ordinance targets advertising with "synthetic" content, including AI-generated or substantially altered images, videos or audio that could misinform viewers about whether the material is authentic. It excludes AI-generated text when featured by itself, as well as content that is "evidently fictional based" in its context or depiction.

Violators could receive a fine up to $300 or a term of imprisonment of up to 30 days. Grzybek and Rose offered the legislation as an effort to prevent voters from being misled. The legislation states that AI has become more proficient in generating imagery that can be difficult or impossible to distinguish from reality, and warns that the technology has also enabled bad actors to spread false information. Rose said the technology and industry are developing fast and government regulation is not keeping up, allowing for some abuses.

Grzybek said in September that exceptions apply to content that does not appear realistic, such as a campaign video in a blatantly cartoon-like style that could not be mistaken for real life. He also said that rather than completely banning AI, which could be considered a violation of the First Amendment, the legislation requires that an advertisement relating to a county elected office have an AI disclosure appear when the content is first presented. The disclosure must be in the same medium as the advertisement and be permanent or extremely difficult to remove. The ordinance does not regulate all uses of AI in political campaigns.

Articles.Title: County Council passes law to regulate AI in Allegheny political ads - TribLIVE.com

stories.Headline: US Navy, Gecko Robotics surge AI maintenance contract to $300M
stories.Summary:
Gecko Robotics announced on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, that the U.S. Navy is increasing the value of its initial contract to up to $300 million. The deal comes just six months after the company reached its first agreement with the sea service. The initial contract began as a 5-year, $54 million indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity deal. Under that deal, Gecko works on 18 ships assigned to the Navy's U.S. Pacific Fleet.

The company uses drones, wall-climbing robots and fixed sensors to gather data on components, decks, welds and hulls. That information, paired with AI tools, is used to identify current and potential structural issues that may remain hidden to the naked eye. A key part of the new investment is Gecko's Komodo machine system, which analyzes the health of deck coatings by scanning and eliminates the need to physically dig into them. This lets the Navy plan repairs and map out damaged areas before a ship enters dry dock, something that previously only happened after the maintenance cycle began. Gecko said in a release that its technology can save the Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and identify structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, reducing inspections from months to days.

Gecko Robotics is the company behind the technology and announced the increased contract value. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle, who adopted the 80% readiness goal from his predecessor Adm. Lisa Franchetti, wrote for Military Times in December that reaching it requires shorter maintenance cycles, increased spare-parts availability, improved training pipelines and targeted upgrades across the fleet.

The Navy has consistently stated its goal of reaching 80% fleet readiness by 2027, despite criticisms of its deployment capabilities. The Government Accountability Office reported in December 2024 that readiness rates among the Navy's amphibious warfare ships fell to 46% between 2011 and 2020, hindering Marine Corps deployment and training plans. In August 2025, that rate reportedly dipped to just 41%, resulting in a more than five-month gap in Marine Expeditionary Unit deployments that year. That gap further strained resources amid the Trump administration's push to counter the illicit drug trade in Latin America and the Caribbean.

Articles.Title: US Navy, Gecko Robotics surge AI maintenance contract to $300M

stories.Headline: Vaisala Xweather Collaborates with NVIDIA to Deliver AI-Powered Early Warning for High-Impact Weather
stories.Summary:
Vaisala Xweather announced a strategic collaboration with NVIDIA on October 21, 2026, during the NVIDIA GTC Berlin event. The collaboration brings NVIDIA Earth-2 and accelerated computing into Vaisala Xweather's observation networks, lightning data and operational weather products. The first use case combines NVIDIA StormScope with Vaisala Xweather's proprietary lightning data to extend lightning forecasting from one hour to three hours of lead time. The companies said this gives customers more time to respond to severe weather.

The change means customers in sectors most exposed to severe weather get two additional hours of warning. These sectors include national meteorological services and government agencies, aviation, energy, maritime, transportation and insurance. The extra time can help move crews to safety, control operations at airports, secure ports and wind farms, or manage crowds at outdoor venues. Vaisala Xweather plans to extend AI-powered warnings to other severe weather and enable more precise high-resolution AI forecasting. The company will bring these services to customers worldwide, from government agencies and national meteorological offices to commercial operators.

Samuli Hänninen, Executive Vice President of Vaisala Xweather, said high-impact weather does not wait and every extra minute of warning matters. He said combining NVIDIA Earth-2 models and AI tools with Vaisala Xweather's observations and expertise can turn advanced models into earlier, more actionable warnings, giving customers more time to protect people, assets and operations. Tim Carroll, Global Weather & Climate Business Manager at NVIDIA, said AI weather models become far more powerful when grounded in real-world observations. He said building on StormScope with lightning data and a global sensor network lets Vaisala Xweather see severe weather coming hours earlier, and the companies are showing how Earth-2 enables operational early warnings that protect lives and livelihoods.

The companies described the collaboration as a landmark strategic effort to advance AI-powered early warning across severe and high-impact weather. Vaisala Xweather said it brings ground truth data, including what it calls the world's most extensive lightning detection datasets, and decades of weather expertise, which no AI model alone can provide. The articles say expanded lightning alerts are the first step in a broader collaboration. Vaisala Xweather said it will help customers modernize forecasting, issue earlier and more confident warnings, and build the future of AI for atmospheric science.

Articles.Title: Vaisala Xweather Collaborates with NVIDIA to Deliver AI-Powered Early Warning for High-Impact Weather

stories.Headline: Samita Helsin Selected to Inaugural Class of the CAA’s Allied AI Collaborative Ambassadors
stories.Summary:
Samita Heslin, a clinical assistant professor of emergency medicine in the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, was named to the inaugural cohort of the Allied AI Collaborative Ambassadors for the 2026-27 academic year. The Coastal Athletic Association Academic Alliance announced the 14 ambassadors on October 21. Heslin was one of them. The Allied AI Collaborative brings CAA Academic Alliance institutions together as a virtual community of learning. The collaborative focuses on three priorities: research and innovation; teaching, learning, and assessment; and ethical and policy considerations.

The 14 ambassadors will facilitate the collaborative’s meetings, deliver presentations, disseminate scholarship, mentor new members and shape the year’s focus areas. The collaborative forms the Alliance’s cross-cutting portfolio of programmatic and research initiatives to advance responsible, innovative and collaborative applications of artificial intelligence across all thirteen member institutions. In February, Heslin and Margaret Schedel were selected by the CAA to help build a conference-wide network about AI-related best practices. Heslin’s work integrates Stony Brook Medicine and the broader university campus and shows how responsible AI can be applied across clinical care, research and interdisciplinary education. She recently led an AI-enabled ambient documentation project in the emergency department to help with clinician workflow and documentation burden.

She also leads the development of AI triage and AI-driven medication safety initiatives. These projects have brought together colleagues in clinical practice, biomedical informatics and computer science. The CAA Academic Alliance was formed in 2002 to academically link the higher education institutions of the CAA. It serves faculty, staff and students across its member institutions through initiatives that enrich the academic environment, advance student success and drive innovation and best practices in higher education. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the ambassadors’ roles for the year.

stories.Headline: UTC computer science team’s AI research paper accepted to NeurIPS 2026 - University of Tennessee at Chattanooga
stories.Summary:
A research team in the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga Department of Computer Science and Engineering has had a paper accepted to the main track of NeurIPS 2026. The paper is titled “SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning.” The UTC authors are Ph.D. students Jingbo Wang and Kegeng Tang, Dr. Zihao Wang, an assistant professor and associate graduate program coordinator, and Dr. Shaogang Ren, an assistant professor and graduate program coordinator. Ren is the paper’s corresponding author and leads the research team and supervises the project.

The conference is the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, and it is scheduled to take place in Sydney, Atlanta and Paris in December. For the 2026 cycle, NeurIPS received 30,709 valid main-track paper submissions and accepted 7,900, an acceptance rate of 25.7%. The team developed SCDM by using meta-learning, an artificial intelligence approach in which a model learns across related tasks, to make the process more efficient. In a system with 3,000 traffic sensors, researchers must consider nearly 9 million possible cause-and-effect links, and existing methods may require a separate model for each variable or many statistical tests.

In simulated brain-imaging data based on a standard map of 100 brain regions, SCDM identified known connections more accurately than six leading methods. In a larger simulation involving about 1 million possible links, it found the correct connections more reliably than a leading recent method in the same amount of computing time. Tested on data from 3,000 Los Angeles freeway sensors, the method ran about 23 times faster than the comparison method and used about one-fourteenth as much graphics-processing-unit memory. Dr. Mengjun Xie, head of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, said the work tackles an important challenge in understanding cause-and-effect relationships in large, complex systems while significantly improving scalability and computational efficiency.

Ren recently received a Ruth S. Holmberg Grant for Faculty Excellence. The research could support work in neuroscience and medicine by helping researchers study how brain regions influence one another in health and disease, and it also could help transportation officials understand how congestion travels through road networks. The approach also could be used to study power grids, environmental monitoring, industrial equipment and financial markets, which all generate large volumes of time-series data. The team’s next steps include enabling SCDM to select its own settings automatically and connecting it more closely with forecasting tools.

Articles.Title: UTC computer science team’s AI research paper accepted to NeurIPS 2026 - University of Tennessee at Chattanooga

stories.Headline: Levy Institute Holds Panel on the AI Bubble, Featuring Pavlina Tcherneva
stories.Summary:
The Levy Economics Institute at Bard College held a Capitol Hill Lecture Series presentation in Washington DC on October 14, titled "The AI Bubble: From Boom to Financial Bust." Zachary Carter moderated the panel, which featured Levy Institute President Pavlina Tcherneva. The panel was cosponsored by the Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. Four panelists discussed whether the artificial intelligence industry is sustainable. Tcherneva focused her remarks on a framework for the financing of the AI buildout, including its fragilities.

She said the job was not to predict the next crisis but to outline the anatomy of a crisis. The panel was followed on October 15 by a Levy Institute briefing with congressional staffers and DC-based think tanks on the topic of the job guarantee. Tcherneva previously published "The Case for a Job Guarantee," which she described as a public option for jobs provided irrespective of the state of the economy. The Levy Economics Institute is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, public policy research organization that encourages diversity of opinion in the examination of economic policy issues.

It says it strives to transform ideological arguments into informed debate. The Capitol Hill Series was established last year and brings together financial experts, academics, and policymakers in Washington, DC. It addresses the most pressing issues facing the US economy. More to follow.

stories.Headline: 5 classic movies that saw our AI future coming
stories.Summary:
Vincent Piturro, a professor of Film and Media Studies at Metropolitan State University of Denver, discussed five films that explored artificial intelligence long before it entered everyday life. The article was published by MSU Denver RED on October 21, 2026, and written by Valeria Quiroz. Piturro said these movies do more than entertain, because they explore questions people now confront in real life. Those questions include who controls AI, whether humans and machines can coexist, and what happens if control is lost.

The five films are 2001: A Space Odyssey from 1968, Blade Runner from 1982, The Matrix from 1999, Her from 2013 and Ex Machina from 2014. In 2001, the computer HAL 9000 turns against its human operators, and Piturro said humans must have some control over AI. The Matrix imagines machines that have taken over the world and use humans as an energy source. Blade Runner raises questions about identity and consciousness through bioengineered beings called replicants, and Her follows a lonely man and an artificially intelligent operating system who calls herself Samantha.

Ex Machina shows a tech billionaire who invites a programmer to evaluate a humanoid AI. Piturro is responsible for the analysis in the article, and he tied each film to a current concern. He said 2001 asks who is in control, and he warned that when AI runs people, they become reduced to its batteries. He said Blade Runner asks whether humans and machines can coexist peacefully.

He said Her asks whether AI will make people lose touch with each other and diminish their humanity, and he called Ex Machina's prospect of machines moving among people undetected possibly the most frightening future. The article says these films explored the same hopes, fears and ethical dilemmas that shape today's conversations about artificial intelligence. Each movie offers a different lens on one of the most important issues of our time, whether it warns about losing control or questions what makes us human. The article does not say what happens next beyond pointing readers to learn about Film Studies at MSU Denver.

Articles.Title: 5 classic movies that saw our AI future coming

stories.Headline: Penn State graduate Igor Jablokov doesn’t want to be ‘a conformist’ in the AI industry
stories.Summary:
Igor Jablokov, a 1997 Penn State computer engineering graduate, founded the AI company Pryon in 2017 and serves as its chairman and CEO. Born in Poros, Greece, the 52-year-old previously worked for decades at IBM and at Yap, which is now part of Amazon, where he played a key role in creating AI programs that became IBM's Watson, Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa. He named Pryon as a tribute to Amazon's codename for Alexa during its development. He said he started the company because nobody was really using AI at work at the time, and nobody really knew what Pryon was working on until ChatGPT came out.

Pryon seeks to create high-performing, resilient and responsive organizations through AI tools such as its ingestion, retrieval and generative engines, according to its site. Jablokov said he wants to use Pryon to explore how natural language experience interfaces can be applied to the workplace, like people creating and modifying computer programs using their voice. He said Pryon also differs from his earlier work with Siri and Alexa by considering AI's applications in places like hospitals and power plants. He originally planned to pursue nuclear engineering when he began at Penn State Abington in 1991 but switched to computer engineering, graduating in 1997, because of a lack of available jobs for nuclear engineers and because computers were being integrated into everyday life.

Jason O'Neill, 50, of Hilo, Hawaii, interviewed with Jablokov in summer 2023 for the chief people officer job and now holds the position. He said the conversation was a very human one that focused more on the humanities and philosophies than on technology, and he described Jablokov as a man with zero ego who insists on sharing credit with the team. Sheridan Clemins, 41, of San Diego, California, Pryon's chief information security officer, has known Jablokov since 2024 and said he finds people he connects with and trusts, gives them freedom and listens when it is time to change or pivot. Jablokov said his leadership style comes from a desire for people to embrace their individuality, recalling that as a student he interviewed in rundown clothes and asked whether he was being hired for his mind or his threads. He advised people not to be just a conformist and to find a unique plot twist so they can show they are one of a kind.

Articles.Title: Penn State graduate Igor Jablokov doesn’t want to be ‘a conformist’ in the AI industry

Ohio schools are creating real-world learning experiences through artificial intelligence problem-solving. The Ohio Department of Education and Workforce hosted the Ohio AI Impact Student Showcase last week. The event was held in partnership with Intel and the Ohio Educational Service Center Association. It highlighted state efforts to combine emerging technologies with teaching and learning.

Students shared projects with educators, industry leaders and community partners. Their work covered a range of subjects. One project was an app to help students create a career plan. stories.Headline: How to Tell an AI What to Do: Rules, Cases, and Interpretation - Berkman Klein Center
stories.Summary:
The Berkman Klein Center will host a talk on how law can guide the written constitutions that AI developers use to govern their most capable models. The event, titled “How to Tell an AI What to Do: Rules, Cases, and Interpretation,” is scheduled for Tuesday, November 3, 2026, from 12:20 PM to 1:20 PM ET. It will take place at 1557 Massachusetts Ave., 5th Floor, Cambridge, MA 02138. Nicholas Caputo and Jordi Weinstock will lead the discussion.

The session will examine what legal theory can and cannot tell us about AI constitutions, which set out a model’s values, priorities and character and are used directly in training. Anthropic’s constitution for Claude is the most prominent example. The talk will ask who has the authority to write these documents and how vague principles should be interpreted when they conflict. It will also ask whether a model can meaningfully consent to the values it is trained on, and what role governments should play.

Caputo is affiliated with the Johns Hopkins School of Government and Policy and the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative. His research treats AI alignment as a problem of jurisprudence, and his work in progress asks whether Claude can consent to its own constitution. Weinstock is at Harvard Law School and the Berkman Klein Center, teaches about the confluence of AI and traditional law, and served as an external reviewer of Claude’s constitution. The two will discuss what legal theory can and cannot tell us about AI constitutions.

The event page lists an in-person RSVP and was last updated on October 20, 2026. It frames the discussion around questions law has dealt with for centuries, including authority, interpretation of vague principles, consent and the role of government. No further details on outcomes or next steps are given. More to follow.
