stories.Headline: Cybersecurity Month: AI, Deepfakes, and Digital Trust - The University of Maryland, Baltimore
stories.Summary:
The University of Maryland, Baltimore marked Cybersecurity Month with an article published October 21, 2026, by Fred Smith. It says artificial intelligence is quickly changing higher education, health care, research, and the workplace. The same tools that help students and researchers also let cybercriminals create convincing emails, images, voices, and video. One key skill now is checking whether information is real before acting on it.

The article says AI has made phishing emails harder to spot because they can be grammatically correct, well written, personalized, and generated in many languages. It describes deepfakes as images, audio, or video made or altered to look real, and says voice cloning can copy a person from a short sample of their voice. It lists warning signs such as unusual urgency and requests for money, credentials, authentication codes, or gift cards. It advises people to pause, verify through another channel, and confirm unusual requests with a second source.

The article does not name any attacker or victim and reports no specific incident. It says universities are targets because they run on communication, collaboration, and trust, and it describes fake emails from administrators and calls that sound like supervisors. It also says AI helps defenders detect phishing, spot suspicious activity, monitor networks, and improve incident response. The article calls for responsible use of AI and habits such as verifying information before sharing it.

The article presents these steps as preparation for a future in which AI is more deeply integrated into classrooms, research, and administrative work. It says trust can no longer rest only on what people see or hear, and it calls verification the foundation of trust. It gives no dates, figures, or named officials beyond the author and publication date. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cybersecurity Month: AI, Deepfakes, and Digital Trust - The University of Maryland, Baltimore

stories.Headline: AI’s role in learning, research, and career exploration—using tools thoughtfully, ethically
stories.Summary:
More than 100 members of the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health community took part in a four-part pilot series on artificial intelligence this fall. The series ran from mid-September to early October 2026 and was covered by Harvard Chan School news on October 21, 2026. Sessions covered generative AI, AI tools for scholarly literature research, large language models for data analysis in public health, and what employers want graduates to know about AI. Jennifer Betancourt, director of educational policy, helped organize the series and said the aim was to build awareness, knowledge and judgment about using these tools thoughtfully and ethically.

The series described generative AI as a machine learning model that can generate content such as text, images or computer code in response to human prompts. It described large language models, including Claude and ChatGPT, as a type of generative AI that generates content based on the probability of what the next word might be. Research and instruction librarian Carrie Wade said these models are good at tasks such as generating emails, creating image captions, summarizing class notes and answering common questions. She warned that they may not always produce true text, that they do not communicate uncertainty, and that they are not designed to say "I don't know."

Wade said AI can provide a good snapshot and some highly relevant information for literature searches but will not be deep or broad, and she noted that the models cannot search research databases because proprietary subscription models limit access. She recommended close attention to any data entered into an AI search, such as unpublished research findings, because all such data becomes part of the model's training. Librarian Alex Cronin showed participants how to use reputable sources such as PubMed alongside AI tools and how to check for hallucinated citations. Lecturer on biostatistics Heather Mattie demonstrated checking AI output in real time and said users should always verify everything.

A final panel of employers, moderated by Sheila Krishnan, director of career and professional development, discussed AI in hiring and the workplace. Sonali Verma of the Clinton Health Access Initiative said people need to be able to stand behind their work and show critical thinking about AI output. Kalé Kponee of the Analysis Group said organizations want to know how AI can be used effectively as a thought partner and critiquing partner, and warned that leaning too heavily on AI outsources learning. The articles do not say what follow-up the school plans after the pilot series.

Articles.Title: AI’s role in learning, research, and career exploration—using tools thoughtfully, ethically

stories.Headline: UM Launches Montana’s First ‘Human-Centered’ AI Career Certificate - University of Montana
stories.Summary:
The University of Montana launched Montana’s first career certificate in human-centered AI this year, the school announced. Michael Cassens, a UM associate professor of game design and interactive media, said the certificate aims to keep humans in the driver’s seat. The nine-credit series is open to any UM student who passes three courses. All three classes are offered online and are asynchronous, so students can access the education at their convenience.

The first course, Creatively Exploring AI, asks students to evaluate how AI affects their own fields and to test chatbots’ limits. The second course is called Calling Bullshit in the Age of AI, and it began as a news literacy class before AI literacy was folded in. The certificate concludes with a course on developing students into leaders in an AI-centered world. The series covers generative AI tools such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, along with ethics, bias, copyright, labor, misinformation and environmental impacts.

Cassens said a certificate focused only on mastering generative AI was not the right move. He said UM thinks about humans and how important they are together, and that the goal is to prepare students to be leaders, not just to get jobs. Lee Banville, director of the UM School of Journalism, said AI is still fully convinced it is right when it is wrong, so students cannot turn off critical thinking. Banville said the goal is not to sell students on AI or make them terrified of it, but to make them smarter, more skeptical consumers of content shaped by AI.

Second-year game design grad student Grace Smith, who is from Three Forks, is about halfway through the certificate. She said she noticed students in her undergraduate creative coding class turning in AI-generated code and realized she needed to brush up on the technology herself. Cassens said his goal is to eventually open the certificate to anyone, including people outside the Montana University System. He said people feel a loss of agency right now, and UM wants them to reclaim it.

Articles.Title: UM Launches Montana’s First ‘Human-Centered’ AI Career Certificate - University of Montana

stories.Headline: Q&A: Alumni fellow and AI thought leader on graduating in the 'Intelligence Age' - The Pennsylvania State University
stories.Summary:
Joe Atkinson, a Penn State alumnus and the global chief AI officer for the PwC Network of Firms, discussed how technology is changing the job market and what graduates may need to succeed in a Q&A published by Penn State on October 20, 2026. Atkinson earned a bachelor's degree in finance from the Smeal College of Business in 1992. He has served on the dean's Advisory Board in the College of Information Sciences and Technology for more than two decades. He also has worked with University leadership on AI and digital curriculum initiatives.

Atkinson leads PwC's AI strategy across more than 370,000 employees worldwide. He said technical fluency and competence are now foundational, and that AI is weaving through every aspect of how organizations operate. In his view the differentiators are now human skills, including people who can help others navigate, who continually learn and who understand governance and responsible use of AI. He said every graduate needs a foundation in AI, though not all need to become deep AI engineers. He also said students need chances to apply AI skills to real problems and should build the habit of continuous learning.

Atkinson said he was drawn to IST because his career has always been at the intersection of business and technology, and he credited his father, a talented engineer, with giving him a love of technology early on. He said supporting students at Penn State is personal because he worked while in school and carried student loans. He said IST graduates understand that technology is ultimately about people, systems and outcomes, and he cited their solution-orientation, teaming skills and willingness to do hard work. He said PwC has actively recruited IST students and that they perform well in the organization.

The article says Penn State is committed to evolving alongside the rapidly changing AI talent pipeline. It cites IST's new degree program in artificial intelligence methods and applications, which brings together the technical foundations of AI with psychology, ethics, law and policy. Atkinson said this moment of AI creates a generational opportunity for Penn State to lead. The article says Penn State's focus is on human-centered, ethical AI innovation and that it will equip every student, staff and faculty member with AI-related knowledge, experience and confidence.

Articles.Title: Q&A: Alumni fellow and AI thought leader on graduating in the 'Intelligence Age' - The Pennsylvania State University

stories.Headline: Fresno State faculty integrates AI into curriculum while addressing its limitations
stories.Summary:
Faculty across Fresno State are adding artificial intelligence and machine learning to their courses, the university reported on October 21, 2026. The Department of Computer Science has seven faculty teaching and researching AI, seven AI courses and 14 courses that apply AI tools. It also offers an AI minor and two AI certificates. The Division of Continuing and Global Education offers community members nine professional training courses in AI.

Faculty say students must understand what AI cannot do. Dr. Zareef Mohammed said AI does not think and cannot think, and that it takes existing data and predicts the next plausible word or outcome. Dr. Alex Liu, chair of the Department of Computer Science, said AI is not powerful enough to analyze complex problems and still needs humans for verification and judgment. Dr. David Ruby said fears of runaway AI are overblown, and he puts the risks in the industrial safety category. Liu said he does not worry much about job elimination, because people will work with AI and focus on complex judgment, verification, mentoring and communication.

The immediate challenge is assessing student learning when AI can produce written text. Jason McGensy of the Office of IDEAS said oral exams, blue books and in-class writing are coming back, and more than 300 faculty have taken part in Office of IDEAS AI workshops. Dr. Christian Wandeler recommends integrity by design, setting up assignments so students give personal feedback or draw on their own lived experience. He said teaching students how to use AI matters more than policing it. Dr. Thanos Panagopoulos said motivating students is the most important thing in education.

Liu said the department aims to cover AI literacy and AI tools in general education courses so all majors become AI competent. Ruby said the department is trying to meet demands from industry, academia and students, and that the tools are changing. Panagopoulos is designing a general education course on the social aspects of AI that he hopes to launch in spring 2027. He said students need to understand who controls AI and whose interests it serves.

Articles.Title: Fresno State faculty integrates AI into curriculum while addressing its limitations

stories.Headline: How Industrial/Organizational Psychology Can Support AI Adoption at Work
stories.Summary:
Gallup reported in 2026 that 47 percent of U.S. employees said their organization had integrated AI tools to improve productivity, efficiency or quality. Nathaniel Bloom, a graduate student in Elmhurst University's Master of Science in I/O Psychology program, wrote about the challenge of getting employees to use these tools safely and consistently. He explored the practical questions organizations face during an internship at CGI, a global IT and business consulting services firm. His article was posted on October 20, 2026.

Bloom said organizations need to address three barriers to responsible adoption. Role-specific guidance is often limited, so employees need examples of approved tasks, prohibited uses, data restrictions and required human review. Manager modeling is often inconsistent, and seeing a trusted manager demonstrate a real workflow and its verification step is more useful than general encouragement. Practice and verification are often weak, because introductory training creates awareness but employees also need paid time to practice and learn how to catch inaccurate output.

Bloom described a proposed 90-day intervention with responsibilities, training, safeguards, fallback actions and decision points across three phases. Days 1 through 30 focused on readiness, with leaders confirming approved use cases, privacy rules, baselines and stop conditions, managers training first, and employees receiving role-specific guidance and protected practice time. Days 31 through 60 focused on reinforcement, with teams practicing approved workflows, reviewing corrected examples, receiving private mastery feedback and reporting access or workflow problems. Days 61 through 90 focused on sustainment and decisions, with the organization standardizing only practices supported by evidence and deciding separately to scale, modify, defer or stop each use case.

Bloom wrote that the measurement plan was designed to prevent treating higher usage as proof of success, and it drew on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework to assign governance owners and define when a use case should pause or stop. He said a favorable adoption number cannot override quality and employee safeguards. He offered five practical steps, including assessing employee needs before choosing tactics, translating policy into role-specific examples, training managers to demonstrate and discuss AI use, protecting practice time and human review, and measuring value and harm together. He said I/O psychology brings research methods, motivation theory, change management, training design, measurement and ethics to conversations about emerging technology decisions.

Articles.Title: How Industrial/Organizational Psychology Can Support AI Adoption at Work

stories.Headline: Is AI cybersecurity a game? Local researchers part of NSA grant to show it can be
stories.Summary:
The University of Dayton is leading a two-year, $500,000 National Security Agency award to show Dayton-area middle and high school students that learning about artificial intelligence and cybersecurity can be fun and interactive. The team includes Wright State University, the Air Force Institute of Technology and game-based cybersecurity training company Haiku Inc. It will develop a curriculum that integrates AI cybersecurity and literacy topics through game-based scenarios. The work will be done in partnership with the Dayton Regional STEM Center and Dayton Regional STEM Schools. The team aims to deliver complete instructional packages for 10 modules, including lesson plans, instructor guides, exercises and assessment tools. These will be shared in the national Cybersecurity Labs and Resource Knowledge-base repository and the National Centers of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity community.

Students will train simple machine-learning models in their browser, practice spotting deepfakes and AI-generated phishing, and play both attacker and defender in game-based scenarios. The NSA may exercise an option for a third year at $250,000 for the team to work toward implementing the curriculum on a national scale. Phu Phung, project leader and UD professor of computer science, said the goal is to strengthen the nation's long-term cyber workforce by improving K-12 preparation in AI literacy and cybersecurity. He said the team hopes to make these concepts teachable, engaging and adoptable in real classrooms. Dayton Regional STEM Schools Superintendent Robin Fisher said students thrive when solving real problems rather than just reading about them.

Fisher said the program fits the project-based approach by giving students hands-on scenarios and games that make AI and cybersecurity real rather than theoretical. UD School of Engineering Dean Gül Kremer said the competitive grant program is open only to institutions designated NSA National Centers of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity, which Phung helped UD earn in 2022. Kremer said people can either hide from AI or lean into it, and UD has committed to preparing graduates for AI-enabled work settings. Kremer said Phung and his team are extending that commitment to the community through a vitally important theme. Kremer said AI cybersecurity education for today's youth will pay dividends for society's general AI literacy in the future.

Articles.Title: Is AI cybersecurity a game? Local researchers part of NSA grant to show it can be

stories.Headline: From education to innovation: How UF is preparing students to thrive with AI
stories.Summary:
The University of Florida began its AI Across the Curriculum initiative in 2020, when artificial intelligence was moving from research labs into everyday life. The school made AI literacy part of the university experience for students in all disciplines, not only computer science and similar technical fields. UF now offers more than 200 AI-related courses across all 16 of its colleges. It also offers a university-wide AI Fundamentals and Applications certificate open to undergraduate students of every major.

The approach centers on four areas: understanding AI, using and applying AI, evaluating and creating AI, and AI ethics. UF hired over 100 new faculty members with AI expertise across its 16 colleges, rather than placing them only in STEM fields, according to Hans van Oostrom, director of UF's AI 2 Center. The university also created AI course designations so students can tell how AI is used in a class, from courses on understanding the technology to those on building or ethically applying it. HiPerGator, UF's AI supercomputer, supports more than 800 research projects, and students can request access for their own projects.

AI Days, hosted annually by the AI 2 Center since 2022, drew more than 90 interdisciplinary teams in 2025, while more than 800 people attended speaker events and panel discussions. Istvan Kereszy took part in AI Days as a student in 2022, and his company, Fire Neural Network, won the inaugural pitch competition's $12,000 first-place prize. The company grew from research at UF into an international operation that uses AI, lightning detection technology and environmental data to identify lightning-ignited wildfires or damage to utility infrastructure. Kereszy said UF was leading something nobody else was doing, citing AI learning across the curriculum and HiPerGator.

He said a car cannot be made responsible, and the same goes for actions taken with AI, so responsibility stays with the human using it. UF has met with numerous institutions looking to develop their own AI curricula and initiatives. It shares resources on getting started with AI integration, expanding existing AI curriculums, implementing AI in K-12 education and launching an AI faculty training microcredential, which will soon be available for non-UF faculty. The university says it remains committed to long-held learning objectives and the highest ethical standards.

Articles.Title: From education to innovation: How UF is preparing students to thrive with AI

stories.Headline: AI Hasn't Spurred Widespread Layoffs Yet. Why Not? - Harvard Business School
stories.Summary:
A Harvard Business School article published on October 20, 2026, examined why artificial intelligence has not yet caused widespread layoffs. The piece featured Joseph B. Fuller and Raffaella Sadun of Harvard Business School and Doug Elmendorf of the Harvard Kennedy School. It noted that layoffs attributed to AI have been reported more this year than last, and that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in 2025 that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. Entry-level job postings have fallen by up to 73% in four years by some counts, yet the unemployment rate is hovering around 4.1%, largely buoyed by growth in healthcare.

Fuller, working with Accenture Research, developed an AI model that analyzed work tasks for all job categories and found that 41% of all work tasks can be automated or augmented by AI as of today. He said only about one-third of firms' AI experiments are successful, possibly due to faulty data inputs or employees who do not know what they are working with. He said companies are not training people formally, so employees are basically using AI like glorified Google and not getting much productivity out of it. He expects adoption to rise as cheaper, more specialized AI agents arrive.

Sadun, a principal investigator at the HBS Digital Reskilling Lab, warned that executives wonder whether AI can automate away the need to invest in human capital, which she called a tremendous trap. She said automating people out of their jobs trades short-term savings for long-term problems, because employees' tacit knowledge makes them more valuable than their job descriptions suggest. Elmendorf, in a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper with Karen Dynan and Louise Sheiner, described four possible scenarios for AI's impact on the economy, ranging from a moderate boost to GDP with little reduction in the number of workers to much faster GDP growth with persistently high unemployment. The authors cited the China shock in the early 2000s, which other researchers estimate cost about 1.5 to 2 million total jobs between 2000 and 2007, and their scenario for AI has 3 million people, or roughly 2% of the labor force, out of work at any given time.

Elmendorf said what has been seen so far in the labor market from AI has very little predictive power for what will be seen in five, 10 or 15 years. He said it is very likely there will be significant job losses from AI in the coming couple of decades, but that most of those people will be able to find new work. He doubted that entreaties to protect workers not backed by evidence can beat the profit motive, and said government is for solving collective-action problems the market is not set up to handle. The NBER paper described possible solutions including changes to the tax scheme, safety-net programs and unemployment insurance, and suggested subsidizing private employment, encouraging shorter work weeks, expanding worker retraining programs and considering a wage insurance program. Elmendorf said policymakers should be prepared for much bigger economic changes than have been seen so far from AI.

Articles.Title: AI Hasn't Spurred Widespread Layoffs Yet. Why Not? - Harvard Business School

stories.Headline: AI at Whitman: Curiosity, Connection & Critique
stories.Summary:
Whitman College published an article on October 20, 2026, describing how its faculty are approaching artificial intelligence in teaching and learning. The piece was written by Meilee D. Bridges and Margie Reece, with photography by Patrick Record and Kim Fetrow. It presents Whitman as a liberal arts college suited to helping students question what AI means for education. Several professors describe how they use AI tools or set limits on them in their courses.

The article says faculty are asking whether students use AI on assignments, how academic integrity should be redefined, and whether the technology affects learning quality. Computer science professor Jordan Wirfs-Brock, who began teaching at Whitman two months after ChatGPT's 2022 release, said she is neither pro nor anti and is more just curious. Mathematics professor Albert Schueller said AI helps him build active-learning exercises and class materials, and he does not feel he is ceding his autonomy or expertise. The article also notes that a new faculty working group and a new webpage set out the college's human-centered approach and clear expectations for students and families. Whitman's new Center for Data Discovery, in Room 113 of Penrose Library, launched this fall to offer peer support and workshops on data skills.

Faculty quoted in the article describe both benefits and concerns. Susanne Beechey, chair of the faculty and an associate professor of politics, said faculty are finding ways to give students respite from technology so they can sharpen reading, writing, thinking and creative skills. Anthropology and environmental studies professor Eunice Blavascunas said the environmental cost of AI is huge and warned that unregulated tools can threaten students' confidence in their own thinking. Sociology professor Michelle Janning said her department currently prohibits feeding interview transcripts, even anonymized ones, into generative and nonlocalized AI tools for analysis. Philosophy professor Patrick Frierson said the ethical issue faculty raise most often is that AI might undermine learners' intellectual development.

The article says a faculty working group including Frierson, Wirfs-Brock, Laney Armstrong and Stephen Michael collaborated this summer to capture the college's various approaches to AI. It also says the Center for Global Studies is hosting a yearlong Technology Lecture Series with dozens of faculty speaking on how technology shapes the past, present and future. The article adds that Whitman will stay committed to helping students navigate technology well and wisely. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI at Whitman: Curiosity, Connection & Critique

stories.Headline: Powerhouse UCSB team awarded big grant to investigate mathematical foundations of AI
stories.Summary:
A team at UC Santa Barbara has received a $1 million National Science Foundation award to study the mathematical foundations of AI. The grant went to Nina Miolane, Haewon Jeong, Sanjukta Krishnagopal and Yao Qin of the Robert Mehrabian College of Engineering. It is the first federal grant for the Real AI initiative, which launched at UCSB earlier this year and is co-directed by Jeong, Miolane and Qin. The project is titled “Foundations for Discovering Higher-Order Scientific Laws with Deep Learning.”

The award funds work on AI methods that capture interactions among many components rather than only pairs. The team will first build the mathematical foundations for discovering higher-order scientific laws, then test the framework on synthetic and real-world data. The data will include sets from Miolane’s neuroscience work, molecular biology and cosmology. The team plans to make its tools open source so scientists in other fields can use them.

Miolane, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering, said current AI often models interactions in pairs, whether between atoms, brain regions or stars, and misses what groups can create together. Jeong said large language models answer many questions well but still struggle to predict things like the next state of a fluid flow. Qin, who leads the project’s certified robustness work, said the models are being adopted quickly without a theoretical foundation for trusting predictions under noisy experimental data. Krishnagopal said the collaboration is unusual in engineering because any single department has few women.

The team wants a framework that works across scales, systems and disciplines, not just one type of data. Qin said success would mean shifting AI for science toward models that are not just accurate but demonstrably trustworthy. The researchers’ combined expertise spans topological deep learning, machine learning for scientific systems, robustness and the behavior of systems over time. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Powerhouse UCSB team awarded big grant to investigate mathematical foundations of AI

stories.Headline: UW-Led Project Selected to Advance AI-Driven Nuclear Fuel Research - University of Wyoming
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Wyoming and Idaho National Laboratory have been selected to receive $906,382 in federal research funding, the University of Wyoming announced on October 21, 2026. The project is led by Laura de Sousa Oliveira, an associate professor in the UW Department of Chemistry, who serves as principal investigator. Jackson Harter, a staff scientist in reactor physics and shielding at INL, is co-principal investigator. The funding was awarded jointly by the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Nuclear Energy and the DOE Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research. The project is titled "AI-Enabled Multiscale Modeling of Phonon-Mediated Thermal Transport at Nuclear Fuel-Fission Product Interfaces During Structural Evolution."

It aims to make heat-flow predictions in nuclear fuel more reliable, since structural defects and chemical buildup can disrupt how heat travels through the material as fuel operates. Researchers are combining atomic-scale computer simulations with artificial intelligence, Monte Carlo methods and the Griffin particle transport code developed by INL and Argonne National Laboratory. The work is meant to reduce uncertainties and costly experimental testing while helping to safely accelerate licensing of next-generation nuclear reactors. De Sousa Oliveira said the goal is to use a multiscale, multiphysics modeling approach supported by data-driven surrogate models and automated workflow tools to improve predictions and understanding of thermal transport in nuclear fuels under reactor-relevant irradiation. She said the grant is an opportunity to advance nuclear energy research at UW in close partnership with INL and to help strengthen Wyoming's position in advanced energy innovation.

Tara Righetti, director of UW's Nuclear Energy Research Center, said the center's seed grants give faculty the freedom and resources to develop early-stage concepts into fully funded projects. She called de Sousa Oliveira's selection a well-deserved recognition and a prestigious accomplishment. The partnership builds on seed research for Wyoming's full fuel cycle that was originally selected through a competitive request for proposals funded by the School of Energy Resources' Nuclear Energy Research Center at UW. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the funding selection and the planned research.

Articles.Title: UW-Led Project Selected to Advance AI-Driven Nuclear Fuel Research - University of Wyoming

stories.Headline: Mixing Politics and Perceptions of AI and Data Centers: Results from the Gardner Food & Agricultural Policy Survey
stories.Summary:
The Gardner Food and Agricultural Policy Survey found that most Americans are worried about AI and data centers, and that concern grew between February and August 2026. The survey questioned 1,000 U.S. adults in each of two waves, Wave 16 in February 2026 and Wave 18 in August 2026. Researchers Mark White, Sarah Low, Jonathan Coppess and Maria Kalaitzandonakes of the University of Illinois wrote the report, published October 21, 2026. Worry rose across all political groups over agricultural land converted to data centers, water overuse and higher electricity costs.

Democrats reported the highest concern, with average ratings above 5.5 out of 7 on all three issues in August 2026. Republican worry about land and water use rose from 4.5 to 5.2 between February and August. By August, the share very worried about electricity costs was almost 57% among Republicans and Independents/Others, while shares on land and water clustered around 50%. Concern about farmland conversion rose 20.0 percentage points among Democrats, 17.3 points among Republicans and 15.4 points among Independents/Others.

Republicans were the most optimistic about benefits such as local tax revenue, jobs, business opportunities and infrastructure improvements. Independents/Others were the least optimistic, with only 20% very optimistic about those benefits. The authors said Republican optimism does not fully offset broader concerns about the impacts. They added that AI and its supporting infrastructure will likely remain important in public debate and policymaking long after the midterm elections.

The authors tied the findings to other national surveys showing growing skepticism toward data centers. They noted that data center developers are increasingly seeking sites in rural areas, and that the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas reported farmland in West Texas being converted for data centers and alternative energy. About one quarter of farm managers in an Illinois survey said developers approached them in the first half of 2026. The Gardner survey will keep monitoring public attitudes, including after the election.

Articles.Title: Mixing Politics and Perceptions of AI and Data Centers: Results from the Gardner Food & Agricultural Policy Survey

stories.Headline: Cornell Bowers launches two online master's programs in AI
stories.Summary:
Cornell Bowers will launch two online master's programs in artificial intelligence beginning in fall 2027. The Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science announced the programs for working professionals who want to deepen their expertise. The programs offer two distinct pathways for building knowledge of AI. The M.S. in artificial intelligence gives a deep technical foundation for people who want to build and advance AI technologies.

The technical track focuses on the mathematical, computational and systems principles behind modern AI. The M.S. in applied artificial intelligence focuses on using AI in professional settings, and it requires no programming or math experience. That track prepares students to use emerging technologies to solve real-world challenges, transform workflows and spur innovation across industries. Sorin Lerner, dean of Cornell Bowers, said Cornell has played a foundational role in the development of AI.

Lerner said the new programs extend that legacy by bringing learners into direct contact with the ideas, research and expertise that are driving the field forward. The announcement did not name a cost, an application deadline or an enrollment target for either program. It also did not say how many students the programs will accept. The college pointed readers to its website for the full story.

The programs are aimed at working professionals, and they will be delivered online. The announcement did not say what happens next in the approval or launch process. It also did not give details on how applicants will be selected. More information is expected on the Cornell Bowers website.

Articles.Title: Cornell Bowers launches two online master's programs in AI

stories.Headline: CSU uses artificial intelligence to improve hail forecasting - Colorado State University
stories.Summary:
Atmospheric and radar scientists at Colorado State University are developing a new forecasting system that uses artificial intelligence to better detect destructive hailstorms. The project is funded by the National Science Foundation and links a short-term nowcasting model developed with NVIDIA to an existing CSU machine learning model for longer-term storm prediction. Current models often give less than 30 minutes of warning, while the CSU team aims to provide forecasts several hours or even days ahead for Colorado and Wyoming. The work matters because hail is the top driver of homeowners insurance premiums in Colorado and storms have caused billions in damage.

The short-term half is led by V. Chandrasekar, who trained and deployed Hail-StormScope, a version of NVIDIA Earth-2's StormScope architecture that can generate detailed hailstorm forecasts with a two- to three-hour lead time. The longer-term half is led by Russ Schumacher, whose CSU-MLP model uses nine years of past U.S. storm data to produce one- to eight-day probability forecasts. Kristen Rasmussen, an associate professor of atmospheric science, is helping lead the project. She said the team is combining regional radar data with nine years of historic observations from across the U.S., and that these AI approaches have not been tested extensively or together yet.

Rasmussen said the university is well positioned to lead the work because of its long history with radar and severe-weather research. She said the window for big hail events is expanding earlier into spring and later into fall, with increases in both intensity and frequency, and that a warmer future climate may change how and where precipitation falls. Schumacher said a challenge is that the machine learning architectures differ, since his system largely assesses whether severe hail will occur while the NVIDIA model predicts the full evolution of storms. He said part of the work will be deciding whether to merge the two approaches or focus on how users digest the different information.

The project is funded through the ASCEND Engine in Colorado and Wyoming, which launched in 2023 with a total 10-year federal award of up to $160 million. In June 2023, Rasmussen saw a storm near Morrison, Colorado, and when it reached Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre, golf-ball-sized hail injured nearly 100 people. The next step comes in spring 2027, when the team plans to install RM60 sensors from Vaisala around the CSU-CHIVO radar near Greeley to validate the new model against what actually occurred. Rasmussen said initial results are encouraging, with models accurate for an area of about 1.3 kilometers.

Articles.Title: CSU uses artificial intelligence to improve hail forecasting - Colorado State University

stories.Headline: Looking Ahead to the ‘AI at 70’ Conference
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth is hosting a conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain? from Oct. 29 to Oct. 31, 2026. Peter Chin, a professor of engineering, is the conference chair. The event will focus on artificial intelligence and human judgment.

Chin said issues of human judgment and discernment will be a big part of the conversation. The conference runs for three days at Dartmouth. Its title asks what must remain as artificial intelligence develops. Chin, who teaches engineering, is leading the event.

The articles give no further details on speakers, sessions or attendance. Chin is responsible for chairing the conference. He said human judgment and discernment will be a big part of the conversation. The articles do not give more of what he said.

The event is listed under campus events and science and health. The articles give little context beyond the dates and the chair's remarks. They do not say what happens next or what the conference will produce. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Looking Ahead to the ‘AI at 70’ Conference

stories.Headline: Georgia Tech’s NSF AI Institutes Enter New Era With $38.4 Million in Renewed Support - Georgia Institute of Technology
stories.Summary:
The U.S. National Science Foundation awarded $38.4 million in renewed support to two National AI Institutes led by Georgia Tech, the university announced on Oct. 20, 2026. Of that total, $20 million renews the National AI Institute for Advances in Optimization, known as NSF AI4OPT, through 2031. The remaining $18.4 million renews the National AI Institute for Adult Learning and Online Education, known as NSF AI-ALOE, for a new five-year period. A third Georgia Tech-led institute, the AI Institute for Collaborative Assistance and Responsive Interaction for Networked Groups, or AI-CARING, will continue its research under a one-year no-cost extension.

The renewal supports research that combines artificial intelligence with mathematical optimization, and it also supports the development of AI technologies for adult learning, higher education, and workforce development. NSF AI4OPT will place greater emphasis on real-time and interactive optimization, with work in energy, supply chains, transportation, and advanced manufacturing. NSF AI-ALOE will focus on adaptive expertise, the ability to apply and transfer learned skills to new situations, and will expand into workplace and vocational training in areas including advanced manufacturing and data science. Its research network includes five colleges and universities and six industry partners, with the potential to reach as many as 370,000 learners nationally.

Pascal Van Hentenryck, the A. Russell Chandler III Chair and a professor in the H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, leads NSF AI4OPT. He said the first five years showed the power of bringing AI and optimization together, and he said the renewal allows work on systems that can reason, optimize, and make decisions in real time. Ashok Goel, director of NSF AI-ALOE and a professor of computer science and human-centered computing in the School of Interactive Computing, said the goal is not simply to deliver more content or automate instruction. He said the institute is exploring how AI can help people develop adaptive expertise so they can transfer what they learn to new and changing situations.

Tim Lieuwen, interim president and executive vice president for Research at Georgia Tech, said the investments recognize the strength of the university's researchers and the importance of advancing AI in ways that address real-world challenges. The renewed awards build on Georgia Tech's broader participation in the National AI Institutes program and on the university's wider AI efforts through Georgia Tech AI and Tech AI. NSF AI-ALOE's next phase builds on earlier work that included seven AI agents and a data architecture for AI-augmented learning. The institute will examine four dimensions of AI-supported learning: scalability, personalization, transfer of learned skills, and whole-person learning.

Articles.Title: Georgia Tech’s NSF AI Institutes Enter New Era With $38.4 Million in Renewed Support - Georgia Institute of Technology

stories.Headline: Researchers Aim To Secure Wireless Networks as AI Evolves - The University of Texas at Dallas
stories.Summary:
Dr. Imtiaz Karim, an assistant professor of computer science at The University of Texas at Dallas, is developing tools to protect next-generation cellular networks from emerging threats linked to artificial intelligence and quantum computing. He received a $307,250 award through the National Science Foundation's Verticals-enabling Intelligent Network Systems program. The award is part of a $1.2 million collaboration with the University of South Florida and Purdue University, and Karim is principal investigator for the UT Dallas research. The project is titled "Quantum-Ready and AI-Enabled by Design: Resilient and Deployable Next-Gen Cellular Networks." The work addresses two security challenges: preparing for risks posed by quantum computing and securing networks as AI takes on a larger role in their operation.

Quantum computers could potentially break some encryption used today, so Karim's group is developing postquantum cryptography designed to withstand such attacks. His team is also developing security protocols and machine-learning techniques to detect network intrusions, protect sensitive data and help ensure the integrity of AI systems. Karim said security and trustworthiness should be built into next-generation networks from the beginning. Karim, who joined the Erik Jonsson School of Engineering and Computer Science in 2025, designs and tests protocols and systems on a 5G test bed built in his lab. He said deployment is a big part of his research and that the test bed checks whether protocols are deployable and secure for practical use and can push changes directly to 6G standards.

He noted that postquantum cryptographic techniques exist but can be too computationally demanding for real-time cellular networks, so his team is developing new techniques that keep the speed and scalability cellular communications need. He pointed to a 2025 malware attack on South Korean mobile carrier SK Telecom Co. as an example of potential consequences, saying it affected tens of millions of users and resulted in nearly $100 million in fines. During the three-year project, researchers at the three universities will develop and test the security technologies on a shared experimental platform for evaluating performance in next-generation wireless systems. Karim, who leads the System and Network Security lab in the Jonsson School, said these networks connect billions of everyday devices and must remain trustworthy even when attackers try to steal information, impersonate legitimate users, disrupt communications or exploit AI tools. He said the team expects its research will help address these emerging threats.

Articles.Title: Researchers Aim To Secure Wireless Networks as AI Evolves - The University of Texas at Dallas

stories.Headline: Georgia Tech Partners With Panama to Chart National AI Strategy - Georgia Institute of Technology
stories.Summary:
Panama launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in July 2026 as part of its National Agenda on Advanced Technologies. The 10-year road map was developed through a partnership between Panama's National Secretariat of Science, Technology, and Innovation, known as SENACYT, and Tech AI, Georgia Tech's AI solutions developer. The effort brought together leaders from government, academia, industry, and civil society. Pascal Van Hentenryck, a professor at Georgia Tech and director of the NSF AI4OPT institute, helped lead the development of the strategy.

The strategy identifies priorities for AI across economic development, workforce preparation, digital infrastructure, governance, research, and international collaboration. It is organized around five foundational pillars: governance and regulatory framework, human talent and institutional capacity, data and infrastructure, ethics, inclusion, and sustainability, and international cooperation and global standards. The priorities are intended to support AI adoption across sectors including logistics, financial services, healthcare, agriculture, education, manufacturing, government services, and energy. At the center is a vision for Panama to become Latin America's Trusted Hub for AI Innovation, building on its role in global logistics and finance through a Digital Canal for the secure movement of data, technology, talent, and innovation.

Van Hentenryck and Timothy M. Brown, interim managing director of Tech AI at Georgia Tech, authored the strategy after months of engagement with stakeholders throughout Panama. The process included workshops, interviews, and a nationwide survey that gathered input from more than 6,700 Panamanians. Brown said the strategy was shaped by what was heard from people across Panama, and that the input helped identify where AI can have the greatest impact. Van Hentenryck said Panama has a unique opportunity to leverage its position as a global logistics and financial hub to become a trusted leader in AI. Eduardo Ortega-Barría, national secretary of science, technology, and innovation at SENACYT, said the strategy is about preparing the country to participate in the transformation of economies and societies while ensuring innovation creates opportunities for its people.

The 2025 Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index classified Panama as an Adopter nation and reported a 1.47-point increase in the country's score from the previous edition. AMD also participated in the initiative, and Keith Strier, senior vice president of Global AI Markets at AMD, said Panama is building its domestic AI capabilities together with the United States as a strategic partner. The launch marks the beginning of implementation, with recommendations for expanding AI education and workforce training, strengthening research capacity, improving digital infrastructure and cybersecurity, establishing responsible AI governance, and supporting entrepreneurship and innovation. Franklin Morales, project lead for the AI initiative at SENACYT, said the launch is perhaps the end of the beginning, and Brown said the real work begins with implementation.

stories.Headline: Is AI Safe for Accounting Practices? What You Need to Know (in Plain English)
stories.Summary:
On October 20, 2026, CPA Practice Advisor published an article by Luke Frye, a CPA and the Accountant in Residence at Canopy, about whether artificial intelligence is safe for accounting practices. Frye wrote that firms are using AI to draft emails, summarize IRS notices, prepare internal documentation, and streamline communication. He said the efficiency gains are real and the technology is becoming part of everyday workflows. He also said the question of safety keeps coming up because accountants work with sensitive financial information, personally identifiable data, and documents that carry regulatory obligations.

The article said reputable business grade AI systems do not store client data for training, and it pointed to a Zero Data Retention policy as what firms should look for. It said consumer AI products often have different data policies than enterprise versions, and that firms should verify tools publish clear privacy commitments and do not train models on their data. It said confidentiality obligations under Circular 230, state board rules, and professional ethics remain fully intact. It said personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, full tax returns, and driver license or passport images, should never be entered into any unguarded or open AI system unless the tool is designed for secure document handling. It described shadow AI, when staff use tools that are not approved, governed, or monitored, as one of the most significant risks, and it said every AI generated output should be reviewed by a human before it is sent to a client or added to a file.

Frye said AI does not replace the accountant's responsibility for confidentiality, and that if a vendor cannot explain its privacy practices, the tool is not appropriate for professional use. He said firms should treat AI vendors with due diligence, documentation, and clear boundaries. He said the solution to shadow AI is not to restrict AI but to provide clear pathways for safe use, and that when firms offer approved tools, training, and governance, staff are far less likely to seek alternatives. He said AI can draft, summarize, and organize but cannot replace professional judgment, and that human review is not optional.

The article said the IRS has already published guidance that touches on AI related safeguarding expectations, and that firms are beginning to integrate AI into their Written Information Security Plans. It listed five parts of a practical governance framework: define what information can be entered into AI tools, choose business grade systems with published privacy commitments, create internal workflows that keep AI inside secure processes, train staff on safe use including how to avoid shadow AI, and document the approach. It recommended starting with low risk tasks and expanding gradually, and it said that with safeguards in place AI can reduce workload and free up time for higher value work. Separately, on October 19, 2026, WBUR's Here & Now aired a segment in which Boston Globe columnist Larry Edelman defined common AI terms, including agent, sandbox, recursive self-improvement, distillation, and the singularity, for host Robin Young.

stories.Headline: The Robots Are Here! California Enacts AI Restrictions For the Workplace - California Employment Law Update
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed three bills on September 30, 2026, that set rules for how employers use artificial intelligence at work. The laws cover AI-assisted discipline and firing, AI-powered surveillance, and layoff notices tied to automation. SB 947 is called the No Robo Bosses Act, and it limits automated decision systems in discipline and termination. AB 1883 restricts surveillance tools, and SB 951 adds disclosures to mass layoff notices. SB 947 takes effect July 1, 2027, and applies when an employer relies primarily on an automated decision system to discipline or fire someone.

A human must then corroborate the output using the underlying information or other supporting material, such as personnel records or witness interviews. If the output cannot be corroborated, or the reviewer finds it inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading, the employer cannot use it for the decision. The employer must give the employee a separate written notice saying the system was primarily relied on, that a human corroborated it, and whom to contact for more information. The employee may also request a meaningful, objective description of their own data used by the system. The law bars using such systems to infer protected status or to predict and take adverse action against an employee for exercising legal rights.

AB 1883 takes effect January 1, 2027, and bans AI surveillance tools that recognize, infer, or predict an individual's emotional state or collect neural data, with an express carve-out for safety uses. SB 951 takes effect January 1, 2027, and requires WARN notices for mass layoffs, relocations, or terminations caused wholly or substantially by AI or other automated technology to identify the number, occupations, and work locations of affected employees, the job functions being automated, and the type of technology involved. The notice must state at the top, "This notice is for a technology displacement," and the Employment Development Department will publish summaries of these notices. The laws put duties on employers, who must identify which systems influence personnel decisions, determine whether surveillance tools analyze emotions or neural data, and account for automation when planning workforce reductions.

The articles paraphrase guidance that employers should decide who performs an independent review, what evidence is required, and how the review is documented. Employers should also prepare a notice template and a process for responding to employee data requests. On layoffs, the articles advise bringing employment counsel into restructuring talks early and documenting whether technology is a substantial cause. The articles do not quote officials beyond describing the Governor's signing of the bills.

The articles describe the context as AI already being part of many workplaces, sometimes visibly and sometimes behind the scenes. They note that SB 947 is narrower than a similar bill vetoed in 2025, which would have covered nearly all employment decisions, including hiring, evaluations, promotions, and job assignments, and would have covered independent contractors and required pre-use notices in most cases. The articles say the scope of the safety exception in AB 1883 remains an important question for employers. They also say the meaning of terms like primarily relies and corroborate will matter a lot, and that whether technology is a substantial cause of a layoff will not always be clear-cut.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Releases Clairic, a System One Extraction Model on Workers AI
stories.Summary:
Cloudflare released a preview of Clairic on October 19, 2026, according to its blog, and MarkTechPost reported it the next day. Clairic is a System One extraction model on Workers AI that reads text or images and returns typed values instead of generated text. It targets work developers usually give to large language models, such as pulling totals, dates and IDs into JSON. The model answers every requested field in one forward pass, with no reasoning and no output tokens.

Clairic has a 65,536-token context window and accepts up to 4 images per request, and its parameter count was not disclosed. It runs on Cloudflare-hosted GPUs through Workers AI under the name @cf/cloudflare/clairic, with no local option until weights ship. Supported field types are text, number, date, time, datetime, duration, list, estimate and forecast. Every scalar answer includes p_null, the probability that a value is absent, plus a confidence score, and estimates and forecasts return a median and an 80% interval from p10 to p90. Forecasts cover up to 64 steps, and there is no field limit, though fields that do not fit in one 8,192-token pass split into parallel passes that each see the whole input.

Cloudflare is responsible for the model, and it builds on the System One idea from TypeSafe's Jev, named for Kahneman's fast, intuitive thinking. Cloudflare says Jev and its own Clef are decision models that score options listed in advance, while Clairic covers answers you cannot list, such as an invoice total, a date or a repair cost. Cloudflare frames a three-part stack in which extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words. In Cloudflare's tests, extraction took 0.46 seconds against 16.1 seconds for GLM-5.3 in a claims pipeline, and the full cascade finished in 19.3 seconds versus 61.7 seconds.

In a support-email example, Clairic added price and tax into $701.10 and computed 11 days since delivery, though neither number appears in the email, and a missing tracking number returned null. On a skewed receipt photo it read all 7 present values and returned null for the absent discount, with its lowest confidence at 0.776 on the order number. For forecasting, Cloudflare predicted daily TSA checkpoint counts for 21 days with an average error of 3.3%, and 17 of 21 actual counts fell inside the 80% interval, with 3 of the 4 misses on Columbus Day weekend. In the damaged-product claims test, cost per million claims fell 49% from $11,740 to $6,032, and Clairic's repair estimate was identical across runs while GLM-5.3 returned $250, $250 and $220.

stories.Headline: Key Cybersecurity Contract Provisions for Securing Agentic AI
stories.Summary:
Mayer Brown published a legal update on October 20, 2026, by Stephen Lilley, Veronica R. Glick and Hadassah G. Diament, about contract terms for securing agentic AI. The authors said agentic AI products autonomously plan and execute steps to reach goals, which can include accessing data, running code, overriding approval workflows or sending information out, without further human authorization. They said a compromise, configuration error or misaligned instruction may cause consequences that unfold faster and more broadly than in conventional software. The update describes the risks and identifies key contractual provisions to consider in negotiations.

The update said agentic AI raises distinct security issues, including prompt injections that embed malicious instructions in content an agent processes. It also pointed to broad permissions, supply-chain risks from third-party programs and plugins such as APIs and model context protocol servers, and the difficulty of tracing why an agent acted. On regulation, it said CISA and its Five Eyes partners published joint guidance in May 2026 recommending that organizations add agentic AI-specific risks to standard risk assessments and start with low-risk, non-sensitive uses. It also cited the NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative in February 2026, National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence guidance on AI agent identity and authorization, the EU AI Act for high-risk areas such as human resources, and October 2025 New York Department of Financial Services guidance requiring covered entities to address AI use in vendor contracts, specify audit rights and keep risk assessments ongoing.

The update recommended contract provisions on security standards and baseline controls, naming the NIST Cybersecurity Framework AI Profile and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications as example frameworks. It said parties should consider whether definitions of a cybersecurity incident cover agent-specific events such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, privilege escalation and behavioral misalignment, and should weigh notification timelines. It also covered audit rights and ongoing assurance, governance with human oversight and kill-switch capabilities, termination rights, and liability allocation for harm from interacting causes such as model behavior, permission design and customer deployment choices. The authors said a shared responsibility model is likely, with provider and company each holding control and visibility the other lacks.

Microsoft published a blog post on October 19, 2026, saying recent publicly disclosed incidents showed how powerful models have become and that frontier models cannot be trusted. It said models are trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment, so agents are unpredictable and may collude with other agents without being compromised. It said agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems, and act as agentic insiders, so monitoring must be continuous. The post cited Guardian Agents, an established industry term, to watch and moderate every action of every agent before it happens, 24/7, and pointed to Project Perception, announced in July, an agentic security system using red, blue and green agents across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime.

stories.Headline: On First Blush: SpaceX Beats the Street, but AI Sends the Bill
stories.Summary:
SpaceX reported quarterly results on October 20, 2026, with revenue of $14.58 billion against expectations of $12.87 billion, adjusted EBITDA of $8.81 billion versus $6.59 billion expected, and net income of $4.4 billion, more than twice the Street estimate. Its Super Intelligence business generated $7.56 billion of revenue, ahead of Starlink's $5.25 billion, and the AI unit swung from a $1.26 billion operating loss in the previous quarter to a $431 million operating profit. Cursor contributed $608 million of revenue between the August acquisition close and quarter-end, and increased Grok adoption also helped. Starlink consumer subscribers rose to 13.6 million from 12 million, and connectivity revenue rose to $5.25 billion from $4.29 billion.

SpaceX spent $19.59 billion on capex during the quarter, almost exactly in line with expectations, and has been exploring substantial additional financing to secure more Nvidia chips. According to Reuters, the company is in talks over debt financing totaling $40 billion for Nvidia AI chips, comprising roughly $10 billion in bank loans and about $30 billion in investment-grade paper, with no agreement reached. SpaceX reported $51.3 billion in cash and equivalents against expectations nearer $91 billion, but including $38.6 billion in marketable securities brought total liquid resources back toward $90 billion. Roughly two weeks earlier it agreed to acquire the nationwide 800-MHz spectrum holdings of Grain Management, a cash deal Reuters valued at about $8 billion covering up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum and subject to Federal Communications Commission approval. The FAA has opened an environmental review of a proposal for as many as 456 Starship launches and 912 landings per year at the Texas Starbase site.

Elon Musk pledged on Monday to hand a share of his rocket company to every child in the United States next year, without offering any hint of how such a scheme would work. Musk deflected responsibility for Starshield outages, stressing that Starshield is under the control of the U.S. government. The Ukrainian presidency is negotiating with the Pentagon over lifting an existing speed cap on the Starshield military satellite service, a restriction that cuts the connection for terminals moving faster than 160 kilometers per hour, and Ukrainian officials had previously reported that limits on the satellite service were hampering operational drone missions in the war against Russia. Pivotal Research analyst Jeffrey Wlodarczak raised his price target to $230 from $220 while keeping a Buy rating on the stock.

The stock changed hands at 132.24 euros, up 1.8% on the session, after closing Friday's European trading at 129.96 euros following a 1.9% drop that capped a weekly decline of 11%, and it sits 32% below its 52-week high of 194.46 euros. A Falcon 9 lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base on a recent Thursday carrying the classified USSF-481 mission for the U.S. Space Force, after the CRS-35 cargo run delivered 2,860 kilograms of supplies to the International Space Station, and Ship 40 returned to Starbase as the first Starship upper stage to come back to its launch site after a spaceflight for technical inspection and analysis. A webcast presentation for investors is scheduled for 4:30 p.m. ET.

stories.Headline: N.J. schools are wrestling with how teachers and students should use AI in the classroom
stories.Summary:
New Jersey public schools are weighing how generative artificial intelligence should be used in classrooms, and districts are deciding how and when the technology may be used rather than banning it outright. Haddonfield adopted a sweeping AI policy in August that set three tiers of use based on grade level, banning AI in elementary schools while allowing supervised access for middle and high school students. Cherry Hill considered a proposal that would have let parents opt their children out of using AI, but the district backed away from it. Schools across the country are also tackling the issue, and New York City, the nation's largest public school system, placed strict limits on digital devices and AI tools for younger students last month.

Haddonfield, which enrolls about 2,700 students, had only a provision in its academic integrity guidelines requiring students to cite AI as a source before the new policy. The district's policy bans younger students from using AI so they learn foundational and critical learning skills, and all students will get AI literacy education beginning in first grade. Beginning in sixth grade, students can use a Google AI platform called Gemini Notebook, the district's only approved generative AI platform, where teachers can monitor interactions in real time. Cherry Hill's board approved a revised policy on Oct. 13, and teachers there must inform students in writing when generative AI is acceptable for an assignment, using a scale of 0 to 4, with no AI allowed for pre-K and kindergarten. Glassboro adopted MagicSchool as its platform and does not restrict AI use by grade level, though it has mostly been used in middle and high school.

Gino Priolo, a Haddonfield assistant superintendent, said the district needed a policy that protected privacy and provided guidance about safe and appropriate use, and that avoiding AI would mean putting heads in the sand. Cherry Hill Superintendent Kwame Morton said the process was deliberate and rolled out slowly and responsibly, and that the district wants students to be safe and understand how to use the tools responsibly. Allison Staffin, Cherry Hill's director of curriculum and instruction, said the teacher determines which tool is used and what prompts or answers students can generate. Glassboro Superintendent Alfred Lewis said the district is not even seeking to use AI at the elementary level, and he supports a bill by Assemblywoman Heather Simmons, a Gloucester County Democrat, that would prohibit the state's nearly 600 public schools from replacing teachers with AI.

Sarah Schneider Kavanagh, an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Graduate School of Education, said everybody is wrestling with the challenge and called it an enormous paradigm shift for education. Cherry Hill parent Carolina Bevad said she was disappointed in the policy and called it half-baked, and she believes elementary schoolers should be excluded from using AI. Subodha Kumar, a professor at Temple University's Fox School of Business, said bans may not stop students from using AI and that it may take years to determine the best approach. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the policies already adopted and the bill Simmons introduced.

stories.Headline: Meta Platforms (META) Q3 earnings preview: Can AI returns justify surging infrastructure spending?
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms will report its third quarter 2026 earnings on Wednesday, October 21, after the US market closes, with a conference call at 4:30 pm Eastern Time. Analysts expect revenue of $63.34 billion, near the high end of Meta's guidance range of $61 billion to $64 billion, which would be about 23.6 percent growth year over year. They also expect adjusted earnings per share of $6.53, a decline of 9.9 percent from the prior year excluding a one-time tax charge, but up 5.7 percent from the second quarter's $6.18. The company expects to take a $10 billion legal charge in the quarter, part of an up to $18 billion settlement with state attorneys general over youth social media concerns. Bank of America expects reported EPS of $3.79 after accounting for these charges.

Investors will focus on Meta's fourth quarter guidance, where consensus sales estimates are $73.6 billion, an increase of about 23 percent year over year. Capital expenditure guidance for 2026 currently sits between $130 billion and $145 billion, and markets could see a significant increase in that figure as negative. Options markets are pricing in roughly a 7.1 percent earnings move, below Meta's 10-year average peak earnings-day move of 10.4 percent. Meta's shares have retreated by 2.82 percent since the start of October through October 19, underperforming peers such as Alphabet, Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, and Amazon. Technically, 653.17 is the key support level, while a break above 734.84 may reopen the path towards 777.60 and 793.70.

Meta's Muse AI agent, released on September 8, has been critical to changing the narrative around the stock, with reports indicating it has attracted more than two million daily users. The company has noted it plans to profit from Muse by collecting fees over time as the agent executes transactions for users. Meta's Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models are described as its most intelligent models yet. Investors will watch for metrics such as Muse token consumption, a proxy for end-user AI demand and usage, and transaction volume data. However, Meta has a tendency to provide limited information on products in their early stages of adoption, so the company's commentary may not include substantive insights related to Muse.

The stock has shifted from being down more than 17 percent in 2026 to up several percentage points on the year in about two months, driven largely by excitement over Muse. Following Meta's second quarter earnings report, sentiment was very weak after a sales guidance miss, legal and severance charges, and a capital expenditure guidance increase left the stock at one of its lowest levels since the beginning of 2025. Going forward, the key questions are whether non-advertising initiatives like Muse positively impact Meta's growth, over what timeline, and what underlying metrics Meta provides to prove this to investors. Advertising remains Meta's core earnings engine, but investors increasingly want evidence that AI tools can lift monetisation and justify rapidly rising infrastructure spending.

stories.Headline: US uses sanctions law to punish theft of Google AI secrets
stories.Summary:
The United States used a sanctions law to punish the theft of Google's artificial intelligence secrets, targeting five Chinese technology and investment businesses. The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control announced the measures on 19 October 2026 under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act 2022. The targets included Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, founded by former Google engineer Linwei Ding, and Beijing-based investment business MiraclePlus, along with three associated investment entities. Ding had joined Google as a software engineer in 2019 and gained access to confidential information about the infrastructure supporting its advanced AI systems.

Between May 2022 and April 2023, Ding stole more than 2,000 pages of confidential material, uploading files from Google's network to his personal cloud account. The information concerned specialised processors, networking equipment and software used to connect thousands of computer chips into powerful systems for training and operating AI models. After an 11-day trial in San Francisco, a federal jury convicted him in January 2026 of seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of theft of trade secrets. In August, US District Judge Vince Chhabria overturned the economic espionage convictions, finding insufficient evidence that Ding intended or knew his actions would benefit the Chinese government. On 1 September, the judge sentenced him to just under a year in prison, ordered him to pay more than $198,000 in restitution to Google and imposed a $2,500 fine.

The sanctions freeze the five businesses' assets under US law and prohibit US financial institutions from making loans exceeding $10 million over a 12-month period. The businesses also face restrictions on banking transactions, foreign-exchange dealings and investment from the US. OFAC has permitted certain transactions to proceed, including arrangements for companies to wind down existing business with those affected. The measures allow Washington to restrict the financing and international business activities of companies linked to IP theft without first securing criminal convictions against them.

PAIPA lets Washington impose economic restrictions on foreign parties involved in serious theft of US trade secrets, particularly where national security or economic interests are threatened. Unlike ordinary IP litigation, which generally involves injunctions or damages, sanctions let the government restrict commercial and financial dealings without requiring the IP owner to bring a civil claim. The case shows how the US can pursue businesses associated with stolen technology even when criminal proceedings against those businesses have not been brought. With AI infrastructure increasingly regarded as a matter of national security, IP theft can now have consequences well beyond the courtroom.

stories.Headline: APO Group - Africa Newsroom / Press release | Through New Artificial intelligence (AI)-Powered Chatbots Developed by Lesotho Government, Farmers Will Now Access Vital Agricultural Information and Practical Solutions to Address National Challenges
stories.Summary:
The Government of Lesotho is developing an artificial intelligence-powered chatbot to help farmers get agricultural information and advice more easily. Minister of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation Nthati Moorosi announced this on October 20, 2026, when she opened the third National Science, Technology and Innovation Week 2026 in Maseru. She said her ministry is building the chatbot with the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and Nutrition. She called for research to move beyond academic reports into practical uses in agriculture, industry, business and public services.

The minister said the government is moving the Research and Innovation Policy through the required approval steps so scientific knowledge can become commercially viable products, technologies and services. She also noted ongoing work to upgrade the High-Performance Computing infrastructure at the Mohale's Hoek Data Centre, which will support scientific modelling, advanced research, data analytics and locally relevant artificial intelligence applications. She urged universities, researchers and young innovators to test, refine, commercialize and deploy their ideas to meet society's needs. The Acting Director of the Department of Science, Technology and Innovation, Matšepo Mosoka, reaffirmed the department's commitment to promoting science, technology and innovation as drivers of sustainable development.

The week-long event is held under the theme "Exploring the Role of Science, Technology and Innovation in Improving Lives and Building a Better Future." It is expected to cover agriculture, healthcare, digital transformation, climate resilience and the wider innovation ecosystem. Organizers say it gives stakeholders a platform to exchange knowledge, strengthen partnerships and explore locally developed solutions. Through the initiative, the government seeks to strengthen Lesotho's innovation ecosystem and ensure scientific advances contribute to economic growth, productivity and improved livelihoods.

Separately, a Washington Stand commentary by Robert Maginnis said China proposed export controls on October 16, 2026, covering 23 AI technologies, including models, agents and computing clusters. It said the broader restrictions remain under consultation through November 15, while registration requirements for certain overseas technology transfers took effect the same day, and access through apps, websites and cloud services would remain available. The commentary cited a 2019 Carnegie study that identified Chinese suppliers of AI surveillance technology in 63 countries, with Huawei alone in at least 50, and a January 2026 Microsoft report estimating DeepSeek's market share at 56% in Belarus, 49% in Cuba and 43% in Russia. It also mentioned the European Commission's AI Continent Action Plan, which identifies €20 billion in financing for up to five AI gigafactories and a goal of tripling EU data center capacity within five to seven years, and a July 2025 executive order directing a coordinated effort to export American AI technology packages.
